ety: Borrowed from French échelon (“rung; echelon”), from échelle (“ladder”) + -on (diminutive suffix). Échelle is derived from Latin scāla (“ladder”), from scandō (“to ascend, climb”), from Proto-Indo-European *skend- (“to jump”).

ex: "That's wonderful! What's his name?" "Elijah." "Wow! A heavy-duty prophet's name!" "Yeah, and he's certainly living up to it."

ety: Borrowed from Latin ēlīminātus, perfect passive participle of ēlīminō (“to turn out of doors, banish”), from ē- + līmen (“a threshold”, līmin- in compounds) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), akin to Latin līmes (“a boundary”); see also English limit and limen.

s.def: To kill (a person or animal).
ex: a ruthless mobster who eliminated his enemies

s.def: To completely remove, get rid of, put an end to.
ex: […] it should be possible to eliminate most of these mental "costs" by improving the e-shopping systems.
Flutter, which is present in most iris-supported lenses, is minimized or virtually eliminated.
Last year, the company eliminated hundreds of jobs and asked some of the remaining staff to take on the responsibilities of those who were let go.

s.def: To render (a facility) unusable, to destroy it; to disable (a soldier), make them unable to fight (typically but not necessarily by killing)
To excrete (waste products).
To exclude (from investigation or from further competition).
ex: Bill was eliminated as a suspect when the police interviewed witnesses.
John was eliminated as a contestant when it was found he had gained, rather than lost, weight.

s.def: To record amounts in a consolidation statement to remove the effects of inter-company transactions.

ety: From Ancient Greek Ἦλις (Êlis).

s.def: A regional unit of modern Greece in West Greece, corresponding to the area once ruled by the city-state.
An ancient Greek city-state in northwestern Peloponnese, modern Greece.

ety: From Latin ēlīsiō (“striking out, forcing out”) (whence -ion (“noun suffix denoting action, result, process, state, condition”)), from ēlīsus (“knocked out, forced out”), past participle of ēlīdō (“to knock, dash or strike out”) (whence elide), from ex- (“out, away”) + laedō (“to strike, collide, hurt”) (whence e- (“assimilated form of ex-”)).

s.def: The deliberate omission of something.
The omission of a letter or syllable between two words or inside a word; sometimes marked with an apostrophe.
ex: See also: contraction, apheresis, apocope, syncope

ety: From Middle English elit, from Old French elit, eslit (“chosen, elected”) past participle of elire, eslire (“to choose, elect”), from Latin eligere (“to choose, elect”), with past participle electus; see elect.

s.def: Of high birth or social position; aristocratic or patrician.
Representing the choicest or most select of a group.
A special group or social class of people who have a superior social or economic status and attendant power, advantages, or privileges in society; a member of such a group.
ex: constituting an elite
the hubris of the elites
Is there a nobler or more disinterested aim than to educate the cadres, the elites of tomorrow?

s.def: An individual member of such a group.
Someone who is among the best at a certain task.
A typeface with 12 characters per inch.

The superior attitude or behaviour associated with an elite.

ety: From Medieval Latin elixir (“philosopher's stone”), from Arabic اَلْإِكْسِير (al-ʔiksīr, “philosopher's stone”), from Ancient Greek ξηρίον (xēríon, “powder for drying wounds”), from ξηρός (xērós, “dry”).

s.def: A substance or liquid which is believed to cure all ills and give eternal life.
A sweet flavored liquid (usually containing a small amount of alcohol) used in compounding medicines to be taken by mouth in order to mask an unpleasant taste.
alchemy: liquid which was believed to turn non-precious metals to gold
A liquid which converts lead to gold.
ex: For Chinese alchemists, gold held the key to the Elixir, the Eastern equivalent of the Philosopher's Stone.

s.def: The alleged cure for all ailments; cure-all, panacea.
A substance which when drunk brings immortality: eternal life, eternal youth.

ety: From Middle English elk, from Old English eolc, eolh (“elk”), from Proto-West Germanic *elh, from Proto-Germanic *elhaz, *algiz (“elk”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élḱis, *h₁ólḱis, variant of *h₁elh₁én, from *h₁el- (“deer”). s.def: Any of various large species of deer such as the red deer, moose or wapiti (see usage notes).
Obsolete form of elke (common swan (Cygnus cygnus, syn. Cygnus ferus)).

ety: From Middle English elle, elne, from Old English eln (“the length of the forearm from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger; a unit of measure”), from Proto-West Germanic *alinu, from Proto-Germanic *alinō, from Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃l-én-eh₂, from *Heh₃l- (“elbow, forearm”). Cognate with Dutch el (“ell”), German Low German Ell (“ell”), German Elle (“ell”), Swedish aln (“cubit; ell”), Icelandic alin (“cubit; ell”), Latin ulna (“forearm”).

s.def: A measure of length. An English ell was 1¼ yards (45 inches or 114 cm), a Scottish ell was about 37 inches (94 cm), a Flemish ell was ¾ yard (27 inches or 69 cm), while certain European ells were less than 50 cm.
ex: A homely proverb recognises the existence of a troublesome class of persons who, having an inch conceded them, will take an ell.
‘Taffety brocade at ten shillings an ell at Simon Snippets, the woman’s tailor, now quite ruined. I shall go distracted.’

s.def: The name of the Latin script letter L/l. (more commonly el)
ex: I have drunk en-ee-cee-tee-ay-ar from the ef-ell-oh-doubleyou-ee-ar-ess in his gee-ay-ar-dee-ee-en many a time.

s.def: An extension usually at right angles to one end of a building.
ex: I could hear them snapping and tearing around, and then one managed to get on the roof by jumping from the low ell.

s.def: Something that is L-shaped.

ety: From French ellipse. Learned borrowing from Latin ellīpsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἔλλειψις (élleipsis). Doublet of ellipsis.

s.def: A closed curve, the locus of a point such that the sum of the distances from that point to two other fixed points (called the foci of the ellipse) is constant; equivalently, the conic section that is the intersection of a cone with a plane that does not intersect the base of the cone.
ex: Near-synonym: oval (synonymous in non-technical use)

s.def: Alternative form of ellipsis: the removal from a phrase of a word which is grammatically needed, but which is clearly understood without having to be stated.
To remove from a phrase a word which is grammatically needed, but which is clearly understood without having to be stated.
ex: In B's response to A's question:- (A: Would you like to go out?, B: I'd love to), the words that are ellipsed are go out.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ellīpsis, from Ancient Greek ἔλλειψις (élleipsis, “omission”). Doublet of ellipse.

s.def: A mark consisting of multiple full stops (with or without spaces), used to indicate omitted, missing, or illegible words; or (in mathematics) that a pattern continues.
ex: The ellipsis in 1, 2, 3, ..., 8, 9 means that the numbers 4, 5, 6, and 7 are not explicitly included, but are considered to be part of the pattern.
The ellipsis in 0.333... means that the number is a repeating decimal, having threes that go on forever.
CARD: Hey Baby. Thanks for the … last night. Love you! HAZEL: Wow. I've never despised an ellipsis so much in my life.

s.def: The omission from a clause of a word or phrase that is nevertheless inferred using the context of the remaining element.
The omission of scenes in a film that do not advance the plot.
ex: It was now possible for writers and directors to cut scenes that did not further the plot; called "ellipses" by filmmakers.

s.def: An ellipse.

s.def: A surface, all of whose cross sections are elliptic or circular (including the sphere), that generalises the ellipse and in Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z) is a quadric with equation x²/a² + y²/b² + z²/c² = 1.
ex: Polarizability can be imagined as a three-dimensional ellipsoid centred on the centre of the molecule, as shown in Figure 10.4.
As mentioned before, modern geodetic datums rely on the surfaces of geocentric ellipsoids to approximate the surface of the earth.

s.def: Such a surface used as a model of the shape of the earth.
ex: Here the geoid is thirty meters below the ellipsoid.

s.def: Shaped like an ellipse; elliptical.
Of or pertaining to an ellipse; elliptic.
Having the tridimensional shape of an ellipse rotated on its long axis.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐλλειπτικός (elleiptikós), from ἐλλείπω (elleípō, “I leave out, omit”). By surface analysis, ellipse + -tic.

s.def: Of or pertaining to an ellipse.
ex: In this chapter, the history of solving elliptic problems by direct marching methods is reviewed.

s.def: That has coefficients satisfying a condition analogous to the condition for the general equation for a conic section to be of an ellipse.
ex: elliptic partial differential equation
elliptic operator
elliptic regularity

s.def: Oval, with a short or no point.
Of, or showing ellipsis; having a word or words omitted; elliptical.
ex: The message, which is elliptic, could be spelled out as: (Hello) Olive. This is Julian. I am here until you want to ring me.

s.def: Of or pertaining to a broad field of mathematics that originates from the problem of calculating arc lengths of an ellipse.
ex: elliptic integral
elliptic function
elliptic curve

s.def: Any function of a complex variable which is periodic in two directions.

ety: From elliptic + -al, from Ancient Greek ἐλλειπτικός (elleiptikós), from ἐλλείπω (elleípō, “I leave out, omit”).

s.def: In a shape of, or reminding of, an ellipse; oval.
Of, or showing ellipsis; having a word or words omitted.
ex: If he is sometimes elliptical and obscure, it is because he has so much to tell us.

s.def: Concise, condensed.
ex: He was called a tramp; but that was only an elliptical way of saying that he was a philosopher, an artist, a traveller, a naturalist and a discoverer.

s.def: Elliptic.
relating to or containing an instance of ellipsis.
An elliptical galaxy.
An elliptical trainer.

ety: From Middle English elme, elm, from Old English elm, from Proto-West Germanic *elm, from Proto-Germanic *elmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élem (“mountain elm”). See also dialectal Low German Elm, dialectal German Ilm, archaic German Ilme, Norwegian and Swedish alm; also Irish leamh, Latin ulmus, Albanian ulzë (“maple”).

s.def: A tree of the genus Ulmus of the family Ulmaceae, large deciduous trees with alternate stipulate leaves and small apetalous flowers.
Wood from an elm tree.
ex: English soldiers handled sturdy bows of yew, ash, or elm, which could propel an iron-tipped arrow as far as a hundred yards.

ety: From Middle English elocucioun, ellocucioun, from Late Latin ēlocutiōnem. Doublet of elocutio.

s.def: The art of speaking, especially public speaking, with expert control of gesture and voice, diction (articulation and word choice), and usage.
ex: perfect elocution
elocution training
study elocution

ety: From Hebrew אֱלֹהִים/אֱלוֹהִים (ʾélôhím, “god(s), heavenly power”), plural of אֱלוֹהַּ (ʾélôah, “god”), often taken to be an expanded form of אֵל (ʾēl, “god”) (whence El).

s.def: God; the name used for God in Hebrew scriptures, and used for the Father by Latter-day Saints.
The extraterrestrial creators of humans; the Raelian gods.

ety: From Late Middle English elongat, elongate (“kept away; different or remote in nature”, adjective), borrowed from Late Latin ēlongātus (“having been stretched out, elongated; prolonged, protracted; having been kept aloof, removed”) + Middle English -at (suffix forming participles). s.def: Elongated, extended, lengthened; (especially biology) having a long and slender form.
ex: Painted turtles lay oval, elongate eggs.
Schwarz had a glass of orange juice in his right hand. He tilted the glass slightly now, the surface of the liquid assuming an elongate outline.

s.def: To make (something) long or longer, for example, by pulling or stretching; to make (something) elongated; to extend, to lengthen.
ex: The maltster cleared his throat in an exaggerated form for emphasis, and elongating his gaze to the remotest point of the ashpit, said, […]
Proceed advanceward for time elongateth itself as many dull Chapel speeches.

s.def: Followed by from: to move to or place (something) at a distance from another thing; to remove.
ex: [L]et the cõmon house of easement [i.e., the outhouse] be ouer some water, or els elongated from the house.

s.def: To become long or longer, for example, by being pulled or stretched; to become elongated.
ex: Here, Mr. Lorry perceived the reflexion on the wall to elongate, and Mr. Cruncher rose and stepped forward.

s.def: Of a plant part: to grow long; also, to have a long and slender or tapering form.

Followed by from: to be at a distance, or move away, from a thing; to depart; (specifically, astronomy) of a planet, star, or other astronomical object: to appear to recede from the sun or a fixed point in the celestial sphere.

ety: From Anglo-Norman aloper (“to abduct, run away”), itself borrowed from Proto-West Germanic *andihlaupan (“to run away”). Equivalent to and- + lope as well as and- + leap (these being doublets). More at lope.

s.def: Of a married or engaged person, to run away from home with a paramour.
Of an unmarried person, to run away secretly for the purpose of getting married with one's intended spouse; to marry in a quick or private fashion, especially without a public period of engagement.
ex: My younger sister has left all her friends-- has eloped; has thrown herself into the power of-- of Mr. Wickham.
"[Molly:] —It was the same last time [You-Know-Who] was powerful, people eloping left right and centre– —Including you and Dad, said Ginny slyly."
Although they had eloped in Vegas, she'd insisted he wear a tuxedo and she buy a wedding dress at one of the local stores.

s.def: Of an unmarried person, to run away secretly from home in order to get married without parental or guardian consent.
To escape from one's caretaker.
ex: Six-year-old Casey eloped during recess and police found him watching traffic lights at the intersection.

s.def: To run away from home (for any reason).

ety: From Middle English eloquence, from Old French eloquence, from Latin ēloquentia. Doublet of eloquency, directly from Latin.

s.def: The quality of artistry and persuasiveness in speech or writing.

ety: From Middle English ells, elles, from Old English elles (“other, otherwise, different”), from Proto-West Germanic *alljas, from Proto-Germanic *aljas (“of another, of something else”), genitive of *aljaz (“other”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos, from *h₂el- (“other”). s.def: Other; in addition to previously mentioned items.

Whatever else she may be, she is not a surgeon.
When all else fails, read the instructions.

s.def: Otherwise, if not.
ex: How else (= in what other way) can it be done?
I'm busy Friday; when else (= what other time) works for you?

s.def: For otherwise; or else.
ex: Then the Wronskian of f and g must be nonzero, else they could not be linearly independent.

ety: From Middle English elswher, from Old English elles hwǣr and elles hwerġen (“elsewhere”); corresponding with else + where. Cognate with Old High German alleswār (“elsewhere”), whence Middle High German alleswā, alswā (“elsewhere”).

s.def: Synonym of somewhere else: in, at, or to some other place.
ex: If you won’t serve us, we’ll go elsewhere.
These particular trees are not to be found elsewhere.

s.def: Synonym of somewhere else: a place other than here.
ex: We are back on the Ligurian coast, from which vertigos push human beings toward all kinds of elsewheres.

ety: From Late Latin ēlūcidātus, perfect passive participle of ēlūcidō (“to lighten, enlighten”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ē(x)- (“out, from”) + lūcidus (“bright, clear, understandable”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), literally “to make light of (something)”, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to see; to shine”). s.def: To make (something) clear and understandable; to clarify, to illuminate, to shed light on.
ex: Let me hear vvhat your ovvn conceptions are of the matter, if they tend to elucidate or reconcile.
The antiquities of France have been elucidated by a learned and ingenious people: […]
The business however, though not perfectly elucidated by this speech, soon ceased to be a puzzle.

s.def: To make (something) lucid (“bright, luminous; also, clear, transparent”).
Clear, understandable.

ety: From Latin ēlūdō (“to evade, elude”), from ē- (“out of”, short form of ex-) + lūdō (“to play; to trick”).

s.def: To evade or escape from (someone or something), especially by using cunning or skill.
ex: The line continued in operation until about 1908, but the precise date of closure has eluded research.
It leaves City still searching for the Champions League, the trophy that has always eluded them

s.def: To shake off (a pursuer); to give someone the slip.
To escape being understandable to; to be incomprehensible to.
ex: I get algebra, but calculus eludes me.

s.def: To escape someone's memory, to slip someone's mind.
ex: The solution of that brainteaser eludes me and the name of the author eludes my memory too.

ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ēlūsiō.

s.def: The act of eluding.

ety: From Latin elutriare (“wash out”), from e- + lutriare (“wash”).

plural of elve

ety: Inherited from Middle English elvisch, from Old English ielfisċ. Equivalent to elf + -ish.

s.def: Of or having to do with elves; elven.

ety: See elvish.

s.def: The language spoken by elves.
ex: These difficult runes are written in Elvish.

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of Elysian.

ety: Attested since 1808. In typography, the em is named after the em quadrat (later called em quad), from m quadrat, a metal type used in letterpress typesetting, which is as wide as the point size of the font.

s.def: The name of the Latin script letter M/m.
A unit of measurement equal to the height of the type in use.
ex: Insert here a one-em dash or long dash.

s.def: A relative unit of sizing defined in terms of the font size.

ety: Borrowed from Latin ēmaciātus, perfect passive participle of ēmaciō (“to make lean, to cause to waste away”), from ex- (“out”) + maciēs (“leanness”), from macer (“thin”).

s.def: To make extremely thin or wasted.
To become extremely thin or wasted.
Emaciated.
Thin or haggard, especially from hunger or disease.
ex: The emaciated prisoners in the death camps were weak and sickly.

s.def: A system for sending messages and datas by means of a computer network, primarily the Internet, using the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol and the Internet Message Format.
ex: He sent me his details via email.
The advent of email has simultaneously brought our society closer together and farther apart.

s.def: A message being sent through email.
ex: He sent me an email last week to remind me about the meeting.
I archive my old emails using a cloud-based service.

s.def: The quantity of messages sent through an email system.
ex: I am searching through my old email.
My inbox used to allow only 50 MB of email at a time until last year, when they upgraded it to 2 GBs!

s.def: An email address.
ex: What’s your email?
In this system, your username is your email.
Don’t send personal messages to my work email.

s.def: A river in Estonia which flows from Lake Võrtsjärv through Tartu County into Lake Peipus, crossing the city of Tartu for 10 km. It has a length of 101 km.

ety: Transliteration of Persian امامقلی (emâmqoli), from Old Anatolian Turkish.

s.def: A transliteration of the Persian male given name امامقلی (emâmqoli)

s.def: To come from a source; issue from.
ex: Fragrance emanates from flowers.
that subsisting form of government from which all special laws emanate

s.def: To send or give out; emit.
ex: […] his baggy, wrinkled suit emanating a diapery stench […]

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin ēmancipātus (“liberated, emancipated”) + English -ate (suffix forming verbs, and adjectives with the sense ‘characterized by the specified thing’). Ēmancipātus is the perfect passive participle of ēmancipō (“to declare (someone) free and independent of another’s power, emancipate; to give (something) from one’s authority or power into that of another, to alienate, transfer; to cause (oneself or someone) to become another’s slave; to make (someone) subservient”), fro…

s.def: To set free (a person or group) from the oppression or restraint of another; to liberate.
ex: to emancipate a colony

s.def: Often followed by from: to free (oneself or someone, or something) from some constraint or controlling influence (especially when evil or undue); also, to free (oneself or someone) from mental oppression.
ex: Education can emancipate us from error or prejudices.
At all events, from that day I was emancipated from modern Puritanism.
Emancipate yourselves from mental slavery, / None but ourselves can free our minds

s.def: To place (something) under one's control; specifically (chiefly reflexive), to cause (oneself or someone) to become the slave of another person; to enslave; also, to subjugate (oneself or someone).
To become free from the oppression or restraint of another.
Synonym of emancipated (“having been set free from someone's control, or from some constraint; at liberty, free”).

ety: From Medieval Latin ēmasculātus, perfect passive participle of ēmasculō (“to emasculate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ē(x)- (“out, from, apart”) + masculus (“male, masculine”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), further from mās (“a man, a male”) + -culus (diminutive suffix).

s.def: To deprive of virile or procreative power; to castrate, to geld.
To deprive of masculine vigor or spirit; to weaken; to render effeminate; to vitiate by unmanly softness.
Of a flower: to deprive of the anthers.
Deprived of virility or vigor; unmanned, weak.

ety: From Middle English enbawmen, from Middle French embaumer, from Old French embasmer. See balm.

s.def: To treat a corpse with preservatives in order to prevent decomposition.
ex: And Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father.

s.def: To preserve.
To perfume or add fragrance to something.

ety: From embalm + -er.

s.def: One who embalms a corpse; a practitioner of mortuary science.
The work of an embalmer.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en-bor. Middle English en- English en- English bank English embank From en- + bank.

s.def: to put up a bank so as to confine or to defend
to protect by a bank of earth or stone

ety: From Spanish embargar (“to arrest”), from late Latin *imbarricāre (“to bar”), from Latin in- + Vulgar Latin *barra (“bar, barrier”).

s.def: An order by the government prohibiting ships from leaving port.
A ban on trade with another country.
ex: Instead he [Jefferson] proposed an embargo, an end to all trade between America and England.

s.def: A temporary ban on making certain information public.
ex: This copy of the federal budget is under embargo until 2 p.m.

s.def: A heavy burden or severe constraint on action or expenditure.
To impose an embargo on trading certain goods with another country.
To impose an embargo on a document.
ex: Embargoed until after first reading in Parliament

ety: Borrowed from Middle French embarquer, from em- + barque (“small ship”). Compare with Portuguese embarcar, Spanish abarcar.

s.def: To cause to go on board a vessel or boat; to put on shipboard.
To go aboard a craft or vessel for transportation.
ex: All passengers please embark now.
[S]ee them embarqued; / And tell me if the VVinds and Seas befriend them.

ety: Borrowed from Latin emporium (“trading station; business district in a city; market town”), from Ancient Greek ἐμπόριον (empórion, “factory, trading station; market”), from ἔμπορος (émporos, “merchant, trader; traveller”) + -ιον (-ion, suffix forming nouns). ἔμπορος is derived from ἐμ- (em-) (variant of ἐν- (en-, prefix meaning ‘in; within’)) + πόρος (póros, “journey; passageway”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to go through; to carry forth”)), modelled after ἐν πόρῳ (en pórōi, “a…

s.def: A city or region which is a major trading centre; also, a place within a city for commerce and trading; a marketplace.
ex: Ning-po, which is situated a short distance westward of Chusan, is the principal emporium of Che-keang province.
Although Hong Kong was not yet a great mercantile mart, it was the major opium emporium east of the Cape of Good Hope.

s.def: A shop that offers a wide variety of goods for sale; a department store; (with a descriptive word) a shop specializing in particular goods.
ex: With a name like “The Wine and Spirits Emporium”, no wonder the prices are so high.

s.def: A business set up to enable foreign traders to engage in commerce in a country; a factory (now the more common term).
The brain.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en-bor. Middle English en- English em- Proto-Indo-European *pótis Proto-Italic *potis Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésti Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- Proto-Indo-European *-t Proto-Indo-European *bʰúHt Proto-Italic *som Proto-Italic *possom Latin posseder. Vulgar Latin potēre Old French pooir Anglo-Norman poerbor. Middle English power English power English empower From em- + power.

s.def: To give permission, power, or the legal right to do something.
ex: Regulations have been made under the Civil Aviation Acts of 1949, 1980 and 1982 which empower Inspectors of Accidents to do these things.

s.def: To give someone more confidence and/or strength to do something, often by enabling them to increase their control over their own life or situation.
ex: John found that starting up his own business empowered him greatly in social situations.
This side of the training is effective in empowering employees to make better decisions on site, and helps to improve employee retention.

ety: From Middle English emperice, emperesse, from Anglo-Norman and Old French empereriz, from Latin imperatrix, equivalent to emperor + -ess. Doublet of imperatrix. Compare modern French impératrice.

s.def: The female monarch (ruler) of an empire.
The wife or widow of an emperor or equated ruler.
The third trump or major arcana card of most tarot decks.
A female chimpanzee.
A deciduous tree, Paulownia tomentosa
A fairy chess piece which combines the moves of the rook and the knight.
Rare form of impress.

ety: From French empressement.

s.def: Animated cordiality; friendliness, enthusiasm.
ex: He grasped my hand with a nervous empressement.

ety: From Middle English emty, amty, from Old English ǣmtiġ, ǣmettiġ (“vacant, empty, free, idle, unmarried”, literally “without must or obligation, leisurely”), from Proto-Germanic *uz- (“out”) + Proto-Germanic *mōtijô, *mōtô (“must, obligation, need”), *mōtiþô (“ability, accommodation”), from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“measure; to acquire, possess, be in command”). Related to Old English ġeǣmtigian (“to empty”), ǣmetta (“leisure”), mōtan (“can, to be allowed”). More at mote, meet. The interconson…

s.def: Devoid of content; containing nothing or nobody; vacant.
ex: an empty purse
an empty jug
an empty stomach

s.def: To make empty; to remove the contents of.
ex: to empty a well or a cistern
The cinema emptied quickly after the end of the film.
The suspected thief was requested to empty her pockets.

s.def: Containing no elements (as of a string, array, or set), opposed to being null (having no valid value).
Free; clear; devoid; often with of.
Having nothing to carry, emptyhanded; unburdened.
ex: And I will giue this people fauour in the sight of the Egyptians, and it shall come to passe that when ye goe, ye shall not goe empty:

s.def: Destitute of effect, sincerity, or sense; said of language.
ex: empty words, or threats
empty promises
[…] words are but empty thanks; my future conduct best will speak my gratitude.

s.def: Unable to satisfy; hollow; vain.
ex: empty pleasures
Ev'n I more sweetly pass my careless days, Pleas'd in the silent shade with empty praise;

s.def: Destitute of reality, or real existence; unsubstantial.
ex: empty dreams

s.def: Destitute of, or lacking, sense, knowledge, or courtesy.
ex: empty brains
an empty coxcomb

s.def: Not pregnant; not producing offspring when expected to do so during the breeding season.
ex: Empty cow rates have increased in recent years.

syn: empty as the tomb on Easter

ety: From empty + headed; compare airheaded.

s.def: Unintelligent.
Silly and lacking sense or discretion; featherbrained or scatterbrained.
ex: Never has a group of actors uttered as many mealy-mouthed platitudes as you'll find bouncing off the walls of this empty-headed film.
Hill, though, captures the entitled, empty-headed viciousness of the wealthy elites the film tries to eviscerate.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en-bor. Middle English en- English em- English purple English empurple From em- + purple.

s.def: To make purple.
ex: Some [wines] deep empurpled as the Hyacine, Some as the rubine, laughing sweetly red, Şome like fair emerauds, not yet well ripened

s.def: To enrage or anger, referring to making the face purple or red with blood.
Of writing, to make overly flowery or showy; to embellish unduly.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐμπύημα (empúēma, “gathering, abscess”).

s.def: A collection of pus within a naturally existing anatomical cavity (as opposed to an abscess, which occurs in a newly formed cavity).

ety: From Latin empyreus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios, “fiery”), from ἐν (en, “en-”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) (English pyre).

s.def: Pertaining to the highest heaven or the empyrean.
Of the sky or heavens.
Fiery, made of pure fire.

ety: From Latin empȳreus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) (whence English pyre).

s.def: The highest heaven, supposed by the ancients to be a region of pure light and fire or else composed of ether, and sometimes seen as the dwelling-place of God or other divine beings; the highest celestial sphere according to ancient and medieval astronomy.
ex: Perchance they mark Where India's cliffs the trembling cloud invade, Or Andes with his fiery banner flouts The empyrean,...

s.def: Of the sky or the heavens, and particularly relating to the highest celestial sphere in premodern cosmology; celestially refined.
ex: Yet upward she [the goddess] incessant flies; Resolv’d to reach the high empyrean Sphere.

s.def: French: empyréen (fr)

ety: Probably from Portuguese ema (“(originally) cassowary; giant rhea; (now) ostrich”).

s.def: A large flightless bird native to Australia, Dromaius novaehollandiae.
ex: From New Holland the emeu, / With his better moiety, / Has paid a visit to the Zo- / ological Society.
I left my young emeus […] just parted from their affectionate father, and not yet fully reconciled to beginning the world on their own account.

s.def: A cassowary (genus Casuarius).

ety: First attested in 1586; borrowed from Latin aemulātus, perfect active participle of Latin aemulor (“to rival, emulate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

s.def: To copy or imitate, especially a person.
ex: People are endlessly fascinating, even if you'd never want to emulate them.

s.def: To feel a rivalry with; to be jealous of, to envy.
ex: But the councell then present emulating my successe, would not thinke it fit to spare me fortie men to be hazzarded in those unknowne regions [...].

s.def: of a program or device: to imitate another program or device
To attempt to equal or be the same as.
Striving to excel, ambitious, emulous.

ety: From Middle French émulation, from Latin aemulātiō.

s.def: Execution of a program or other software designed for a different system, by simulating parts of the other system.
The endeavor or desire to equal or excel someone else in qualities or actions.
ex: a great figure who is worthy of respect and emulation

s.def: Jealous rivalry; envy; envious contention.
A person or thing that emulates.
A piece of software or hardware that simulates another system.

ety: From Middle English emulous, from Latin aemulus (“striving to equal or excel, rivaling; in a bad sense, envious, jealous”) + -ous, from Ancient Greek ἁμιλλάομαι (hamilláomai, “strive, contend”), akin to Latin imitari (“to imitate”); see imitate.

s.def: Ambitious or competitive.
ex: A dozen emulous young persons in, or just out of, pinafores, swift-runners, had taken the field.

ety: Etymology tree English emulsify Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English emulsifier From emulsify + -er.

s.def: A substance that helps an emulsion form, or helps keep an emulsion from separating.
ex: The lecithin in egg yolks is often used as an emulsifier.

ety: From Latin ēmūnctus, past participle of ēmungō (“to blow one's nose”) + -ory.

s.def: Pertaining to the elimination of waste from the body.
ex: A mixture of poor diet and poor hygiene caused him inflammation of the emunctory aperture.
This guy was extremely hirsute. Everywhere. So much I used to wonder how he could clearly manage certain emunctory functions.

s.def: Any part of the body which carries or removes waste.

ety: The name of the letter comes from Latin en. The typographic sense dates to 1793.

s.def: The name of the Latin script letter N/n.
ex: The word length, which contains only four sounds l e ng th, is usually spell'd thus, el ee en gee tee aitch.
I have drunk en-ee-cee-tee-ay-ar from the ef-ell-oh-doubleyou-ee-ar-ess in his gee-ay-ar-dee-ee-en many a time.

s.def: A unit of measurement equal to half an em (half the height of the type in use).

ety: An unadapted borrowing from French en passant.

s.def: In passing, by the way, incidentally.
Of a capture of an enemy pawn, by moving one's pawn to the square that the enemy pawn has just passed over.
A move in which a pawn captures an opposing pawn on the same rank immediately after the latter has moved forward two squares on its first move in the game, as if it had moved forward only one square.
ex: Spectators are privy to awe inspiring castles, baffling forks, and breathtaking en passants.
Before he returns to performing some castles and en passants, [Kendall] Williams has to determine his endgame in the tourney.

ety: From Middle English en- (“en-, in-”). Originally from Old French en- (also an-), from Latin in- (“in, into”) and Frankish *in-, *int-, *anda-; but also from an alteration of in-, from Middle English in-, from Old English in- (“in, into”), from Proto-Germanic *in (“in”). Both the Latin and the Germanic forms are from Proto-Indo-European *en (“in, into”). Intensive use of Old French en-, an- is due to confluence with Frankish *an- and *in- (intensive prefixes), related to Old English on- and in-…

s.def: Forms a transitive verb whose meaning is to make the attached adjective
ex: embathe, enquire, enlist

s.def: to become
ex: enslave, embetter, engloom

s.def: provide with
an intensifier
ex: entangle, enwisen, enhance

ety: From Middle English enablen, equivalent to en- + able.

s.def: To activate, to make operational (especially of a function of an electronic or mechanical device).
To make somebody able (to do, or to be, something); to give sufficient ability or power to do or to be; to give strength or ability to.
To affirm; to make firm and strong.
To qualify or approve for some role or position; to render sanction or authorization to; to confirm suitability for.
To yield the opportunity or provide the possibility for something; to provide with means, opportunities, and the like.
ex: Temperance gives Nature her full play, and enables her to exert herself in all her force and vigor.
During 1971-72, spare Type 4s on other regions enabled the whole class to be sidelined, with Class 43s going first.

s.def: To imply or tacitly confer excuse for an action or a behavior.
ex: His parents enabled him to go on buying drugs.

s.def: To put a circuit element into action by supplying a suitable input pulse.

ety: From Middle English enhablement, equivalent to enable + -ment.

s.def: The act of enabling.

ety: From Middle English enacten, from en-, from Old French en- (“to cause to be”), from Latin in- (“in”) and Old French acte (“perform, do”), from Latin actum, past participle of ago (“set in motion”).

s.def: To act the part of; to play.
ex: I did enact Julius Caesar.

s.def: To do; to effect.
ex: The king enacts more wonders than a man.

s.def: To make (a bill) into law.
ex: The practical effect of the Government's new anti-strike bill on the rail disputes in Great Britain is awaited, after the legislation was enacted.

ety: From Middle English enamel, from Anglo-Norman enamailler, from en- (“in-”) + amailler (“to enamel”), variant of Old French esmailler (“to enamel”), from esmal (“enamel”), from Early Medieval Latin smaltum, from Frankish *smalt, from Proto-Germanic *smeltaną (“to melt, smelt”).

s.def: An opaque, glassy coating baked onto metal or ceramic objects.
A coating that dries to a hard, glossy finish.
The hard covering on the exposed part of a tooth.
A cosmetic intended to give the appearance of a smooth and beautiful complexion.
To coat or decorate with enamel.
To variegate with colours, as if with enamel.
ex: Oft he [the serpent] bowed / His turret crest and sleek enamelled neck.

s.def: To form a glossy surface like enamel upon.
ex: to enamel card paper; to enamel leather or cloth

s.def: To disguise with cosmetics, as a woman's complexion.

ety: From enamel + -er.

s.def: A person who applies enamel, especially a craftsman who applies decorative enamel

ety: From Middle English enamouren, a late back-formation from enamoured, itself a partial calque of Old French enamore, past participle of enamorer, enamourer, equivalent to prefix en- + amor + -er. See amour, and compare inamorato.

s.def: To cause to be in love.
ex: Me-thought I was enamoured of an Asse.

s.def: To captivate.
ex: Passionately enamoured of this shadow of a dream.

ety: Inherited from Middle English enamoured, a partial calque of Old French enamore, past participle of enamorer, enamourer; compare amour and enamor, enamour.

s.def: In love, amorous.
ex: She's enamored of [or with] her new boyfriend.

s.def: A ball-and-socket joint.

ety: From Latin ēnātus.

s.def: A relative whose relation is traced only through female members of the family.
ex: A great-grandmother is an enate if she is your mother’s mother's mother.

s.def: Any maternal female relative.
Related to someone by female connections.
Related on the maternal side of the family.
Having identical grammatical structure (but with elements that are semantically different).
Growing out.

ety: From en- + cage.

s.def: To lock inside a cage; to imprison.
ex: Bruce's daughter, Marjory, and his sister Mary, were likewise to be encaged, the former in the Tower of London, the latter in Roxburghe Castle.
I feared the sight of encaged animals would be unbearably sad.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en-bor. Middle English en- English en- English camp English encamp From en- + camp.

s.def: To establish a camp or temporary shelter.
To form into a camp.

ety: From en- + capsule + -ation or encapsulate + -ion.

s.def: The act of enclosing in a capsule; the growth of a membrane around (any part) so as to enclose it in a capsule.
Grouping together an object’s ‘state’ (its data) and the operations that may alter or interrogate it (its methods).
The process of arranging data into packets that can be transmitted using a given protocol.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en-bor. Middle English en- English en- English case English encase From en- + case.

s.def: To enclose, as in a case.
ex: And with the story of the booking office, we have a fortune deeply entwined with the stations encasing them.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐγκαυστικός (enkaustikós, “burning in”), from καίω (kaíō, “to burn”).

s.def: Prepared by means of heat; burned in.
ex: After all, no sealant or finish is necessary in the encaustic medium, and shellac is stinky, caustic and messy.

s.def: A wax-based paint that is fixed in place by heating.
ex: It has become usual in discussions of Flags facture to use the terms, suggested by [Jasper] Johns himself, ‘encaustic', oil and collage on fabric’.
I have worked in encaustic and I really love encaustic printmaking, but when it comes to painting, I love my acrylics.

s.def: A painting produced using this type of paint.

ety: Borrowed from French enceinte.

s.def: Pregnant.
ex: And the time was pressing, for the new queen was enceinte, and further concealment was not to be thought of.

s.def: An enclosure.
ex: And so across the bridge and into the enceinte of the massive walls, threading their way towards the quarter where the morgue lay.

s.def: The line of works forming the main enclosure of a fortress.
The area or town enclosed by a line of fortification.
ex: S. W. Williams The suburbs are not unfrequently larger than their enceinte.

ety: From Latin Enceladus, from Ancient Greek Ἐγκέλαδος (Enkélados).

s.def: A moon of Saturn.
ex: Such cryovolcanism probably occurred on Saturn's moon Enceladus (below right), where ices oozed through fissures.

s.def: A giant in Greek mythology.

ety: From encephalon + -ic.

s.def: of or relating to the encephalon

ety: From encephal- + -itis.

s.def: Inflammation of the brain.

ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐγκέφαλος (enképhalos, “within the head”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).

s.def: The area of central nervous system that includes all higher nervous centers, enclosed within the skull and continuous with the spinal cord; synonym of brain.
ex: Meronyms: prosencephalon, telencephalon, diencephalon; mesencephalon; rhombencephalon, metencephalon, myelencephalon

ety: From encephalo- + -pathy.

s.def: Any of various conditions affecting the brain.
ex: Repeated trauma or shaking to the brain can be even worse, leading to chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en-bor. Middle English en- English en- Proto-Italic *katesnā Latin catēna Old French chaeinebor. Middle English cheyne English chain English enchain From en- + chain.

s.def: To restrain with, or as if with, chains.
ex: [B]y this sign one enchained the demons of the air, the spirits of fire, the phantoms of water and ghosts of earth.

s.def: To link together.

ety: From Middle English enchaunten, from Old French enchanter, from Latin incantāre. Doublet of incant.

s.def: To attract and delight, to charm.
To cast a spell upon (often one that attracts or charms).
To magically enhance or degrade an item.
An enchantment
Having the ability to enchant; charming, delightful.

ety: From Middle English enchauntement, from Old French enchantement.

s.def: The act of enchanting or the feeling of being enchanted.
Something that enchants; a magical spell.
ex: Bodin, the medieval demonographer, enumerates various methods of producing anaphrodisiac effects by enchantments.

ety: From Middle English enchacen, enchasen, from Middle French enchasser.

s.def: To set (a gemstone, etc.) into.
ex: The woods before and behind me made a square frame of silence, and I was enchased here in the clearing, thinking of all things.

s.def: To be a setting for.
ex: My ragged rimes are all too rude and bace, / Her heauenly lineaments for to enchace.

s.def: To decorate with jewels, or with inlaid ornament.
To cut or carve, as with a weapon.

ety: From Spanish enchilada, past participle of enchilar (“to add chili pepper to”).

s.def: A Mexican dish made by wrapping a filling in a tortilla, then baking in a sauce.
ex: It was a nice little pub in the middle of nowhere / Anywhere would have been better / I ordered enchiladas and I ate 'em

ety: Either via Latin enchīridion or directly, from Ancient Greek ἐγχειρίδιον (enkheirídion, “handbook, manual”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + -ίδιον (-ídion).

s.def: A handbook or manual.
ex: the Enchiridion of Erasmus

s.def: A cartilage cyst found in the bone marrow.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐγχώριος (enkhṓrios, “rural, in or of the country”), from χώρα (khṓra, “country”).

s.def: Indigenous, native.
Of, relating to, or written in the Egyptian Demotic script or language.
ex: The inscription of the Rosetta Stone is written in hieroglyphics and in enchorial letters, with a Greek translation.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en-bor. Middle English en- English en- English cipher English encipher From en- + cipher.

s.def: To convert plain text into cipher.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en-bor. Middle English en- English en- Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-der. Middle English circle English circle English encircle From en- + circle.

s.def: To surround, form a circle around.
ex: "Friday!" she called out, bursting open the doors and quickly encircling her friend in the warmth of her arms.

s.def: To move or go around completely.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en-bor. Middle English en- English en- Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-der. Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos)bor. Latin circus Proto-Indo-European *-lós Proto-Indo-European *-elós Proto-Italic *-elos Latin -ulus Latin circulus Old French cerclebor. Middle English circle English circle English encircle Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥tom Proto-Italic *-mentom Latin -mentum Old French -ment…

s.def: The act of encircling or the state of being encircled
The isolation of a target by the formation of a blockade around it

ety: Borrowed from French enclave, from Middle French enclave (“enclave”), deverbal of enclaver (“to inclose”), from Old French enclaver (“to inclose, lock in”), from Vulgar Latin *inclāvāre (“to lock in”), from in + Latin clavis (“key”) or clavus (“nail, bolt”). Compare inlock.

s.def: A political, cultural or social entity or part thereof that is completely surrounded by another.
ex: The Republic of San Marino is an enclave of Italy.
The streets around Union Square form a Protestant enclave within an otherwise Catholic neighbourhood.

s.def: A group that is set off from a larger population by its characteristic or behavior.
An isolated portion of an application's address space, such that data in an enclave can only be accessed by code in the same enclave.
ex: When an enclave spans a system boundary in a sysplex, it is called a multisystem enclave.

s.def: To enclose within a foreign territory.

ety: From Late Latin encliticus, from Ancient Greek ἐγκλιτικός (enklitikós, “inclined towards”), from ἐγκλίνειν (enklínein, “lean on”), from ἐν (en, “upon”) + κλίνειν (klínein, “to lean, incline”).

s.def: A clitic that joins with the preceding word phonetically, graphically, or both.
ex: The English possessive 's is an enclitic.

s.def: Affixed phonetically.

ety: From Middle English enclosure, from Old French enclosure, from enclore, from Latin inclūdere, inclūdō, from in- (“in”) + claudō (“to shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂u- (“key, hook, nail”). Alike to inclusion.

s.def: Something that is enclosed, i.e. inserted into a letter or similar package.
ex: There was an enclosure with the letter — a photo.
Mr Carlyle cut open the envelope, glanced at the enclosure, and in spite of his disappointment could not restrain a chuckle.

s.def: An area, domain, or amount of something partially or entirely enclosed by barriers.
ex: He faced punishment for creating the fenced enclosure in a public park.
The glass enclosure holds the mercury vapor.
The winning horse was first into the unsaddling enclosure.

s.def: The post-feudal process of subdivision of common lands for individual ownership.
ex: Strip-farming disappeared after enclosure.
'[…] The inclosure of Norland Common, now carrying on, is a most serious drain. […]'

s.def: The act of enclosing, i.e. the insertion or inclusion of an item in a letter or package.
ex: The enclosure of a photo with your letter is appreciated.

s.def: The act of separating and surrounding an area, domain, or amount of something with a barrier.
ex: The enclosure of public land is against the law.
The experiment requires the enclosure of mercury vapor in a glass tube.
At first, untrained horses resist enclosure.

s.def: The act of restricting access to ideas, works of art or technologies using patents or intellectual property laws.
The area of a convent, monastery, etc where access is restricted to community members.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en-bor. Middle English en- English en- Latin caudex Latin cōdex Old French codebor. Middle English code English code English encode From en- + code.

s.def: To convert (plain text) into code.
ex: encode a secret message to be sent

s.def: To convert source information into another form.
ex: The blotchy black mark she impresses on my hand will still be there tomorrow morning, a confused barcode, unsure of what exactly it encodes.

s.def: To constitute the code necessary for the biosynthesis of a protein by means of a matrix so as to transcribe DNA material.
An encoding operation.
ex: When each encode is finished a notification will appear on your screen to let you know it's completed […]

s.def: A device or algorithm used to encode something.
A sensor which converts a position into an electronic signal.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐγκωμιαστής (enkōmiastḗs).

s.def: A person who delivers an encomium or eulogy.

ety: From Latin encōmium (“praise, eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐγκώμιον (enkṓmion, “laudatory ode, praise”), from ἐγκώμιος (enkṓmios, “of or pertaining to the victor”), from κῶμος (kômos, “festival, revel, ode”).

s.def: Warm praise, especially a formal expression of such praise; a tribute.
ex: "I never seen their like," was Lassiter's encomium, "an' in my day I've seen a sight of horses."
Many a new locomotive class has received encomiums in these columns because its early work was outstanding, judged by the then prevailing standards.

s.def: A general category of oratory.
A method within rhetorical pedagogy.
The eighth exercise in the progymnasmata series.
A genre of literature that included five elements: prologue, birth and upbringing, acts of the person's life, comparisons used to praise the subject, and an epilogue.

ety: From Middle English encompassen. By surface analysis, en- + compass.

s.def: To form a circle around; to encircle.
To include within its scope; to circumscribe or go round so as to surround; to enclose; to contain.
ex: Beauty is complicated; it’s an individual response to how we live our lives – but it can also encompass kindness and compassion.
Mayor Andy Burnham's Bee Network already encompasses the buses and trams, and now he has his sights set on the railways.

s.def: To include completely; to describe fully or comprehensively.
ex: This book on English grammar encompasses all irregular verbs.

s.def: To go around, especially, to circumnavigate.
ex: Drake encompassed the globe.

ety: Borrowed from French encore (“more, again”), and once used in this sense.

s.def: A brief extra performance, done after the main performance is complete.
ex: To play an encore.
Can I get an encore? We want more!

s.def: A call or demand (as by continued applause) for a repeat performance.
ex: The encores were numerous.

s.def: Please perform again!
To call for an extra performance or repetition of, or by.
ex: to encore a performer
to encore a song

s.def: To call for an encore.
To perform an encore.
ex: They encored with a cover of the Beatles' “Blackbird,” “The Bigger You Love” in 1970, and “Ha Ha Ha” in early '71.
Truly unbelievable. Left us all gasping for breath, and wanting more. I think they encored twice, but twenty encores would have been too few.

ety: From Middle English encountren, from Anglo-Norman encountrer, Old French encontrer (“to confront”), from encontre (“against, counter to”), from Late Latin incontrā (“in front of”) itself from Latin in (“in”) + contrā (“against”).

s.def: To meet (someone) or find (something), especially unexpectedly.
ex: H' incounters Talgol, routs the Bear, / And takes the Fidler Prisoner; / Conveys him to enchanted Castle, / There shuts him fast in wooden Bastile.

s.def: To confront (someone or something) face to face.
To meet one another.
ex: […] yet when the brother and the sister had encountered, according to the set appointment, none of these impassionedments had been repeated.

s.def: To engage in conflict, as with an enemy.
ex: Three armies encountered at Waterloo.
I will encounter with Andronicus.

s.def: To kill or execute someone extrajudicially.
A meeting, especially one that is unplanned or unexpected.
ex: Their encounter was a matter of chance.
As they have planned the encounters, they mostly have control over the time limits.

s.def: A hostile, often violent meeting; a confrontation, skirmish, or clash, as between combatants.
A match between two opposing sides.

A sexual encounter; sexual activity, especially unplanned or unexpected, between two people who have not already established a sexual relationship with each other. In many cases, it does not lead to a relationship, and thus is utterly transient. A sexual encounter can be consensual or non-consensua…
ex: Though Mr. Cosby described the sexual encounter in 2004 as consensual, Ms. Constand said she was too intoxicated to physically or verbally resist.

s.def: The period of a space mission during which it carries out its data-gathering objectives.

ety: From Middle English encouragen, encoragen, from Anglo-Norman encoragier, from Old French encoragier. Displaced native Old English hiertan, tyhtan, and trymman. By surface analysis, en- + courage.

s.def: To spur on, strongly recommend.
ex: We encourage the use of bicycles in the town centre.
We encourage you to cycle instead of taking the car.

s.def: To foster, give help or patronage.
ex: The royal family has always encouraged the arts in word and deed.
In addition the Marquess built a brickworks adjacent to the colliery, and also greatly improved the harbour to encourage coastal shipping.

s.def: To mentally support; to motivate, give courage, hope or spirit.
ex: I encouraged him during his race.
Delia's coach encouraged her to focus on the positives.
The visitors we do not encourage are the many small boys who slip in unobserved and are a danger to themselves and the staff.

s.def: Giving courage, confidence or hope; auspicious.
ex: Although there is no cure for the disease yet, the research results are encouraging.
There are some encouraging signs of economic recovery.

s.def: Supporting by giving encouragement: positively.
ex: Your encouraging words inspired me to persevere.

s.def: present participle and gerund of encourage
encouragement
ex: […] the thousand little ties of sympathy and mutual hopes and fears, comfortings and encouragings.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en-bor. Middle English en- English en- English crimson English encrimson From en- + crimson.

s.def: To make crimson or redden.

ety: From Middle English encrochen, from Old French encrochier (“to seize”), from Old French en- + croc (“hook”), of Germanic origin. More at crook.

s.def: to seize, appropriate
To intrude unrightfully on someone else’s rights or territory.
ex: Because change itself would absolutely stay-stable, and again, conversely, stability itself would change, if each of them encroached on the other.
I won’t encroach on your time any longer.
He never allows work to encroach upon his family life.

s.def: To advance gradually beyond due limits.
Encroachment.
ex: All that we see, all colours of all shade, By encroach of darkness made?

ety: From en- + -crypt, from Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, literally “hidden, concealed, private, secret”).

s.def: To conceal information by means of a code or cipher.
ex: All messages on this platform are doubly encrypted to increase security.

s.def: To transform information using encryption in a way that it is believed only authorized parties can decode.
ex: The data was encrypted in transit using AES-GCM.

s.def: Being in code; having been encrypted.
ex: The encrypted text was unreadable.

ety: From Middle English encombren, from Old French encombrer, from en- + combrer (“to hinder”) (See cumber). By surface analysis, en- + cumber.

s.def: To load down something with a burden.
To restrict or block something with a hindrance or impediment.
ex: He [Timothy Forsyte] had never committed the imprudence of marrying or encumbering himself in any way with children.

s.def: To burden with a legal claim or other obligation.
Weighted down, loaded sufficiently to make slow.
ex: A ship loaded with too much cargo is encumbered.

s.def: Burdened by financial debt, mortgages, or other legal obligations.

ety: From Middle English encombraunce, from Old French encombrance, from encombrer.

s.def: Something that encumbers; a burden that must be carried.
Alternative spelling of incumbrance (“in law: interest attached to a title; dependent”).
The state or condition of being encumbered.
Furniture or other large household item, especially when used or as waste.

ety: From Late Latin encyclicus + -al, from Ancient Greek ἐγκύκλιος (enkúklios, “circular, general”), from ἐν- (en-) + κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”).

s.def: A papal letter, intended for general circulation in the Catholic Church.
Intended for general circulation.

s.def: A comprehensive reference work (often spanning several printed volumes) with articles (usually arranged in alphabetical order, or sometimes arranged by category) on a range of subjects, sometimes general, sometimes limited to a particular field.
ex: I only use the library for the encyclopedia, as we’ve got most other books here.
My old encyclopedia has been gathering dust on the shelf for the past decade.
It would be easier to compile an encyclopedia for you than to write these longhand letters whose ink blackens the night.

s.def: Similarly comprehensive works in other formats.
ex: Wikipedia is an online encyclopedia that anyone can edit.
The ancient Mesopotamians never got to write an encyclopedia on stone.
To gain market share, Microsoft gave away its CD-ROM encyclopedia with many new computers, a strategy similar to those it has used in other areas.

s.def: The circle of arts and sciences (see Etymology); a comprehensive summary of knowledge, or of a branch thereof.
ex: His life's work is a four-volume encyclopedia of aviation topics.
I have no idea how to build this model railroad, so I'm gonna look it up on Trainpedia, the encyclopedia for all things model train.
Since the publication of the second edition of the encyclopedia, there have been numerous developments in the obesity and eating disorders field.

s.def: Of or relating to the characteristics of an encyclopedia; concerning all subjects, having comprehensive information or knowledge.

Relating to or containing descriptive information rather than only linguistic or lexical information; about facts and concepts, and not only a word or term; including proper names, biographical and geographical information and illustrations.

s.def: A member of a group of French authors who collaborated in the 18th century in the production of the Encyclopédie, under the direction of Denis Diderot.
An author of, or contributor to, an encyclopedia.
ex: The root of the mallow in goat's milk excites the sexual urge, according to Pliny the Elder, the Roman encyclopedist of the first century A.D.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en-bor. Middle English en- English en- Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH-? English cyst English encyst From en- + cyst.

s.def: To enclose within a cyst.
To be enclosed within a cyst.
ex: ‘Six months for the projectile to encyst before the knee can be opened safely.’

ety: From Middle English ende, from Old English ende, from Proto-West Germanic *andī, from Proto-Germanic *andijaz (“end”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entíos (“forehead; front”), from *h₂ent- (“face; forehead; front”), from *h₂en- (“on, onto”). Cognates Cognate with Yola een, eene (“end”), Saterland Frisian Eend, Eende (“end”), West Frisian ein (“end”), Alemannic German End, Endi (“end”), Central Franconian Eng, Enk (“end”), Cimbrian énte (“end”), Dutch eind, einde, end (“end”), German Ende (“end”)…

s.def: Death.
ex: He met a terrible end in the jungle.
I hope the end comes quickly.
Confound your hidden falsehood, and award / Either of you to be the other's end.

s.def: The most extreme point of an object, especially one that is longer than it is wide.
ex: Hold the string at both ends.
My father always sat at the end of the table nearest the kitchen.

s.def: Result.
ex: O that a man might know / The end of this day's business ere it come!
The end was that he was thought an archfool.

s.def: A purpose, goal, or aim.
ex: For what end should I toil?
The end of our club is to advance conversation and friendship.
But, losing her, the End of Living lose.

s.def: To finish, terminate.
ex: The referee blew the whistle to end the game.
And on the seventh day God ended his worke[…]
But play the man, stand up and end you, / When your sickness is your soul.

s.def: The terminal point of something in space or time.
ex: An epidemic of the disease started in Lü-shun at the end of 1927 and extended to April 1928, involving 271 cases with 14 deaths (Migai, 1928).
At the end of the garden there was a beautiful fountain.
At the end of the story, the main characters fall in love.

s.def: Share of joint responsibility.
ex: Are you sure they'll honor their end of the deal?

s.def: The cessation of an effort, activity, state, or motion.
ex: Is there no end to this madness?

s.def: One of the two parts of the ground used as a descriptive name for half of the ground.
ex: The Pavillion End

s.def: The position at the end of either the offensive or defensive line, a tight end, a split end, a defensive end.
ex: Her husband, among various physical accomplishments, had been one of the most powerful ends that ever played football at New Haven […].

der: all good things come to an end
all good things must come to an end

s.def: Any change that seems catastrophic or devastating.
ex: You make it sound as though moving house is the end of the world.

s.def: The death and destruction of life on Earth, especially human.
The destruction of Earth.
Synonym of ends of the earth (“a faraway place”)
The final consumer of a product; the intended recipient or user.
ex: Measuring site health from the end user's point of view is the discipline of EUEM, which is the logical complement to web analytics.

ety: From end user + license + agreement.

s.def: A contract between the manufacturer or copyright holder, also commonly called the licensor, of an end product and a person, commonly called the end user, that specifies the licenses under which the end user may utilize the end product, subject to restrictions as specified in the contract or agreeme…

ety: From Middle English endamagen, from Old French endamagier.

s.def: To damage.
ex: Ne ought he car'd, whom he endamaged / By tortious wrong, or whom bereau'd of right.
My picture vanish'd, vanish feares, / That I can be endamag'd by that art […].

ety: From en- + danger. Displaced native Old English frēcnian.

s.def: To put (someone or something) in danger; to risk causing harm to.
ex: I hold him but a fool that will endanger / His body [in a duel] for a girl that loves him not
All the other difficulties of his reign only exercised without endangering him.

s.def: To incur the hazard of; to risk; to run the risk of.
ex: He that turneth the humours back […] endangereth malign ulcers.

s.def: in danger, at risk, said of something where there is a strong possibility something bad will happen to it (for example, a species in danger of going extinct)
ex: I have but done my devoir, lady, as a good knight, in defence of an endangered maiden […]

s.def: A species which is in danger of becoming extinct throughout all or a significant portion of its range.
ex: The federal government has added five more birds to the endangered species list.

s.def: A class or kind whose continued existence is threatened.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en-bor. Middle English en- English en- English dear English endear From en- + dear.

s.def: To make (something) more precious or valuable.
To make (something) more expensive; to increase the cost of.
To stress (something) as important; to exaggerate.
To make (someone) dear or precious.
ex: By giving candy to the children the man tried to endear himself to them.

ety: The verb is from Middle English endeveren (“to make an effort”); the noun is from Middle English endevour, from the verb. Endeveren is from (putten) in dever (“(to put oneself) in duty”), from in + dever (“duty”), partially translating Middle French (se mettre) en devoir (de faire) (“(to make it) one's duty (to do), to endeavour (to do)”) (from Old French devoir, deveir (“duty”)).

s.def: A sincere attempt; a determined or assiduous effort towards a specific goal; assiduous or persistent activity.
To attempt through application of effort (to do something); to try strenuously.
ex: She was endeavoring to teach us the elements of a good prose style.

s.def: To exert oneself.
To attempt (something).
To work with purpose.

Old French -iquebor. Middle English -ik English -ic English endemic From Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”) + δῆμος (dêmos, “people”) + -ic. Possibly via Ancient Greek ἔνδημος (éndēmos, “among one's people, at home, native”) and/or French endémiq…

s.def: Prevalent in a particular area or region, persistent within a population.
ex: Malaria is endemic to the tropics.

s.def: Native to a particular area or culture; originating where it occurs.
ex: The endemic religion of Easter Island arrived with the Polynesian settlers.

s.def: Peculiar to a particular area or region; not found in other places.
ex: Kangaroos are endemic to Australia.

s.def: An individual or species that is endemic to a region.
ex: The species that appeared as a consequence were endemics; that is, they were found nowhere else in the world.

s.def: A disease affecting a number of people simultaneously, so as to show a distinct connection with certain localities.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”) + -ic.

s.def: Acting through the skin, or by direct application to the skin.
ex: endermic application of medicine

ety: From Middle English endynge, endyng, endinge, from Old English endung, ġeendung (“ending”), equivalent to end + -ing. Cognate with Dutch ending (“ending”), German Endung (“ending”).

s.def: A termination or conclusion.
The last part of something.
ex: The book has a happy ending.
The film has an unexpected ending.

s.def: The last morpheme of a word, added to some base to make an inflected form (such as -s in "dogs").
ex: Spanish verb forms have different endings depending on the tense, mood and person.

s.def: present participle and gerund of end

ety: From Middle French endive, from Medieval Latin endivia or Italian indivia~endivia, from Byzantine Greek ἐντύβιον (entúbion), from Latin intibus (which see). The ultimate source is likely Semitic.

s.def: A leafy salad vegetable, Cichorium endivia, which is often confused with common chicory (Cichorium intybus).
ex: Take the three heads of endive out of the water, drain them, and leave the largest whole.
Endive, like a number of similar plants, is both esculent and reputed to have some aphrodisiac property.
Endive and escarole are the same vegetable, but endive has leaves that are cut and curled, while escarole has smooth, broad leaves.

ety: From Middle English endeles, from Old English endelēas (“endless”), from Proto-Germanic *andijalausaz (“endless”), equivalent to end + -less.

s.def: Having no end.
ex: endless time; endless praise
Trains from Lime Street to Edge Hill were hauled by an endless hempen rope worked by a stationary engine on the platform at the latter station.

s.def: Extending indefinitely.
ex: an endless line

s.def: Too much or many to be exhausted; an extremely high number or amount of; immeasurable, innumerable.
Without profitable end; fruitless; unsatisfying.
ex: All loves are endless.

ety: From Old English andlang ( > along), re-formed by popular etymology in Middle English as end + long; partly from Old Norse cognate endlangr.

s.def: Along (as opposed to across), from end to end of.
From end to end.
Continuously.
ex: The rest he leaves in ground: So takes in hond To seeke her endlong both by sea and lond

s.def: On end.

Middle English -most English -most English endmost From end + -most.

s.def: last in a series, furthest away
ex: There was a woman sitting in the endmost chair just across the aisle in line with them.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥dóm Proto-Hellenic *éndon Ancient Greek ἔνδον (éndon)der. English endo- From Ancient Greek ἔνδον (éndon, “inner; internal”).

s.def: Alternative form of end-.

ety: Etymology tree English endocard(ium) Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek -της (-tēs)der. Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis)lbor. New Latin -itisder. English -itis English endocarditis From endocard(ium) + -itis.

s.def: An inflammation of the endocardium and sometimes also the heart valves.
A thin serous membrane that lines the interior of the heart.

ety: From endo- + -carp.

s.def: The woody inner layer of the pericarp of some fruits that contains the seed: the tissue (uncountable) or the structure that it composes (countable).
ex: Holonyms: pyrena < drupe, stone fruit

ety: From French endocrine, from endo- + Ancient Greek κρίνω (krínō, “to separate, also to secrete”).

s.def: Producing internal secretions that are transported around the body by the bloodstream.
Pertaining to the endocrine glands or their secretions.
The secretion of an endocrine gland.
An endocrine gland.
A control system of ductless glands that secrete hormones which circulate via the bloodstream to affect cells within specific organs.

ety: Etymology tree English endocrinology Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Hellenic *-tās Ancient Greek -τής (-tḗs) Ancient Greek -ῐστής (-ĭstḗs)bor. Latin -istader. Old French -istebor. Middle English -ist English -ist English endocrinologist From endocrinology + -ist.

s.def: A person who is skilled at, or practices, endocrinology.
ex: Some endocrinologists argue that our core understanding of T, as a fundamentally male sex hormone, is inherently flawed.

ety: From endo- + -derm.

s.def: One of the three tissue layers in the embryo of a metazoan animal, which will produce through development, the digestive system of the adult.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥dóm Proto-Hellenic *éndon Ancient Greek ἔνδον (éndon)der. English endo- English lymph English endolymph From endo- + lymph.

s.def: The watery fluid inside the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear.

ety: Etymology tree English endometrium Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Hellenic *-tis Ancient Greek -τῐς (-tĭs) Ancient Greek -σῐς (-sĭs) Ancient Greek -ωσις (-ōsis)bor. New Latin -ōsislbor. English -osis English endometriosis From endometrium + -osis.

s.def: A generally painful condition characterised by the presence of endometrial-like tissue in places other than the lining of the uterus; an instance of such tissue being present.
ex: The cyclic changes characterizing endometrioses are particularly apparent in endometriosis of the bladder.
One can treat all adnexal diseases including cysts and endometrioses of the rectovaginal septum.

ety: (physical type): Derived from endoderm + -morph from William Herbert Sheldon. Equivalent to endo- + -morph.

s.def: A mineral, especially a crystal, enclosed within another
A person of the endomorphic physical type, characterised by big bones, round face, large trunk and thighs and a naturally high degree of body fat, especially around the midsection.
A person having a theoretical body type with slow metabolism in which weight is gained easily, but fat levels are hard to reduce. Endomorphic bodybuilders tend to be the most massive.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥dóm Proto-Hellenic *éndon Ancient Greek ἔνδον (éndon)der. English endo- Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Hellenic *pərai Ancient Greek πᾰρᾰ́ (părắ) Ancient Greek σῖτος (sîtos) Ancient Greek παράσιτος (parásitos)der. Latin parasītusder. Middle French parasite English parasite English endoparasite From endo- + parasite.

s.def: A parasite that lives inside the body of an organism, such as a tapeworm.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥dóm Proto-Hellenic *éndon Ancient Greek ἔνδον (éndon)der. English endo- English -plasm English endoplasm From endo- + -plasm.

s.def: The inner portion of the cytoplasm of a cell.
A network of membranes within the cytoplasm of cells, where proteins and lipids are synthesized.

ety: PIE word *h₁én From English endo- (prefix meaning ‘internal, inside, within’) + Ancient Greek ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow, gush, stream”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *srew- (“to flow, stream”)) + English -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining’ to forming adjectives).

s.def: Of a basin or lake: having no outflow to an external body of water such as a river or ocean, and only losing water through evaporation or seepage into the ground.
ex: In the floor of the Rift Valley most of the streams are affected by the tectonic disturbances and are mostly fault-guided besides being endoreic.
