ety: From Middle French épique, from Latin epicus, from Ancient Greek ἐπικός (epikós), from ἔπος (épos, “word, story”).

s.def: An extended narrative poem in elevated or dignified language, celebrating the feats of a deity, demigod (heroic epic), other legend or traditional hero.
ex: The Icelandic epic took all night to recite.

s.def: A series of events considered appropriate to an epic; any work of literature, film, etc. having heroic deeds and adventures as its subject matter.
ex: The book was an epic in four volumes.
These epics nearly always had runaway trains, nincompoops floundering with the controls and a collapsed bridge just ahead!

s.def: A large or extended user story.
Of or relating to an epic.
ex: Beowulf is an epic poem.
The main theme of epic poetry is, of course, the hero, his life, his greatness of character, his deeds and his death.

s.def: Momentously heroic; grand in scale or character.
ex: The epic defense was rewarded with the highest military decorations
China's epic traffic jam "vanished" [title of article]

s.def: Extending beyond the usual or ordinary.
ex: The after-prom party was truly epic.
You made an epic mistake.
Then tell him his daughter's an epic shag.

s.def: That is an epimorphism.

ety: New Latin, from Latin epi- (“over”) + Ancient Greek καρδία (kardía, “heart”). Attested in English from the 19th century.

s.def: The layer of tissue between the pericardium and the heart.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin epicēdīum. Doublet of epicede.

s.def: An epicede: a dirge, lament, elegy.

ety: From Late Middle English epicene, epicen, epicin, epcyn, episcen, epycen, epycene, epycyn, ypsen (“(grammar) having only one form for masculine and feminine gender, common”), from Late Latin epicoenos, epicoenus (“of a noun: applicable to either males or females”), Latin epicoenon (“noun applicable to either males or females; grammatical gender of such nouns”), from Ancient Greek ἐπίκοινος (epíkoinos, “common to many people, things, etc.; promiscuous, sluttish”) (compare γένος ἐπίκοινον (génos…

s.def: Of or relating to a class of Greek and Latin nouns that may refer to males or females but have a fixed grammatical gender (feminine, masculine, neuter, etc.).
ex: In many names of animals, the same word with the same gender is used for both sexes: ἡ ἁλὠπηξ the fox, male or female. These are said to be epicoene.

s.def: Of or relating to nouns or pronouns in any language that have a single form for male and female referents.
Suitable for use regardless of sex; unisex.
Of indeterminate sex, whether asexual, androgynous, hermaphrodite, or intersex; of a human face, intermediate in form between a man's face and a woman's face.
ex: There is a kind of aesthetic masturbation here akin to Elmer's love of impregnable, virginal epicene women.
‘The actor was male. He wasn’t one of Jim’s regulars. But the character I recognize in the door is epicene.’

s.def: Indeterminate; mixed.
Of a man: effeminate.
An epicene word; preceded by the: the epicene words of a language as a class.
An epicene person, whether biologically asexual, androgynous, hermaphrodite, or intersex; an androgyne, a hermaphrodite.
A transsexual; also, a transvestite.
ex: Of Transvestites and Other Epicenes [article title]

s.def: An effeminate man.

ety: From epi- + center.

s.def: US standard spelling of epicentre.
ex: Before the area was a tech epicenter, it was a bucolic land of fruit orchards.

s.def: US standard spelling of epicentre.

ety: From epi- (“over, on top”) + centre, from Ancient Greek ἐπί (epí, “on”) + κέντρον (kéntron, “centre”). Sense of “center of an activity (particularly a disaster)” (1908) by generalization from earthquakes, possibly influenced by epidemic.

s.def: The point on the land or water surface directly above the focus, or hypocentre, of an earthquake.
ex: The epicentre isn't always the point of heaviest damage. Faults can be many kilometres long and seismic waves shake areas all along the fault.

s.def: The point on the surface of the earth directly above an underground explosion.
The focal point of any activity, especially if dangerous or destructive.
The geographical area in which an ongoing disaster, illness, crisis, or other destructive event is currently most severe.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐπίκρισις (epíkrisis, “determination, decision; judgment, award”).

s.def: A critical or analytical study, evaluation, or summing up, especially of a medical case history.
ex: But what if I don't have time to discharge you tomorrow. The epicrisis has to be written, you know.
Haberal’s epicrisis report, which was prepared on Oct. 16, 2009, was sent to the court nearly one year later.

s.def: A quotation followed by a commentary.
A commentary or annotation of a text.
A Roman census in Egypt related to the determination of liability for poll tax.

ety: From Epicurus, the name of an Ancient Greek philosopher who advocated such a lifestyle.

s.def: A person who takes particular pleasure in fine food and drink.

ety: From Epicurean (“follower of Epicureanism”).

s.def: Pursuing pleasure, especially in reference to food or comfort.
Devoted to luxurious living.
One who is devoted to pleasure.

ety: From Epicurean + -ism. As a pejorative synonym of atheism, both from the philosophy's rejection of deontological morality and from Epicurus's specific belief that the Greek gods—if they did exist—did not concern themselves at all with mankind, its actions, or any system of reward or punishment for them. Doublet of epicurism.

s.def: The philosophical belief that pleasure is the highest good, particularly as advocated by Epicurus with a focus on mental pleasures and on avoidance of pain (ataraxia) through moderation and common virtue.
Synonym of hedonism, general pursuit of pleasure, particularly refined and knowledgeable enjoyment of good food, drink, and similar sensual pleasures.
Synonym of atheism.

ety: From Latin Epicūrus, from Ancient Greek Ἐπίκουρος (Epíkouros).

s.def: An ancient Greek philosopher, founder of the movement known as Epicureanism.

ety: From French épidémique, from épidémie, from Medieval Latin epidēmia, reanalysis of plural Late Latin epidēmia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδήμιος (epidḗmios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + δῆμος (dêmos, “people”). By surface analysis, epi- (“on”) + demic (“of the people”).

s.def: A widespread disease that affects many humans in a population.
An occurrence of a disease or disorder in a human population at a frequency higher than that expected in a given time period; an episode of outbreak and subsequent high prevalence.
A heightened occurrence of anything harmful.
The spreading of an idea or belief amongst a population.
Of, related to, or being an epidemic: a widespread outbreak of disease in humans.
Like an epidemic: widespread in a bad way.
ex: Epidemic hysteria occurred upon the incumbent’s reelection.
The major reason for such an examination was to determine if any patterns uncovered seemed to be more epidemic than endemic.
This proportion increased about 5% from 1988 to 1992—hardly a change of epidemic proportions.

ety: From Late Latin epidemia + -logy. See epidemic for more.

s.def: The branch of science dealing with the spread and control of diseases, viruses, concepts etc. throughout populations or systems.
The epidemiological body of knowledge about a particular thing.

ety: Borrowed from Latin epidermis, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδερμίς (epidermís), ἐπί (epí, “on top of”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”). Equivalent to epi- + dermis.

s.def: The similar outer layer of cells in invertebrates and plants.
skin's outer layer in animals
The outer, protective layer of the skin of vertebrates.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐπιδιδυμίς (epididumís), from ἐπί (epí, “upon, over”) + δίδυμος (dídumos, “twin; testicle”).

s.def: A narrow, tightly-coiled tube connecting the efferent ducts from the rear of each testicle to its vas deferens, where sperm are stored during maturation.
ex: Most men, I daresay, have never heard of their epididymis.

ety: From epididymo- + -itis (“inflammation”).

s.def: inflammation of the epididymis

ety: From epi- + focal.

s.def: epicentral

ety: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting New Latin combining forms. By surface analysis, epigastrium + -ic = epi- + gastr- + -ic = epi- + gastric.

s.def: Of or relating to the epigastrium.

s.def: A cartilaginous organ in the throat of terrestrial vertebrates covering the glottis when swallowing to prevent food and liquid from entering the trachea, and in Homo sapiens also a speech organ.
ex: My epiglottis is full of bees!

ety: From Middle French epigramme, from Latin epigramma, from Ancient Greek ἐπίγραμμα (epígramma, “inscription”).

s.def: A brief but witty saying.
An inscription in stone.
A short, witty or pithy poem.
ex: The second has written a sonnet upon the mutability of woman, And the third writes an epigram to Candidia.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐπιγραφή (epigraphḗ, “inscription”), from ἐπιγράφω (epigráphō, “write upon”), from ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “on, upon, over, etc.”) + γρᾰ́φω (grắphō, “to draw, paint, write, etc.”).

s.def: An inscription, especially on a building.
A literary quotation placed at the beginning of a book or other text.
The set of all points lying on or above the function's graph.
To provide (a literary work) with an epigraph.

ety: From epigraph + -y.

s.def: The study or decipherment of inscriptions, especially of ancient ones.
Inscriptions collectively.

ety: From French épilation.

s.def: The removal of hair from the skin in such a way that removes or destroys the root.
The removal of hair from the skin via the use of an epilator.

ety: From epilate + -or.

s.def: An electrically-powered device used for hair removal by mechanically grasping multiple hairs simultaneously and pulling them out.

ety: Since 16th century; borrowed from French épilepsie, from Latin epilēpsia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιληψίᾱ (epilēpsíā), from ἐπιλαμβάνω (epilambánō, “to seize”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) + λαμβάνω (lambánō, “to take”). Displaced native Old English fiellesēocnes (literally “falling sickness”).

s.def: A medical condition in which the sufferer experiences seizures (or convulsions) and blackouts.
ex: Epilepsies, or fallings and reelings, and beastly vomitings. The least of these, even when the tongue begins to be untied, is a degree of drunkenness.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French epilogue, from Latin epilogus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίλογος (epílogos, “a conclusion, peroration of a speech, epilogue of a play”), from ἐπιλέγω (epilégō, “to say in addition”). Eclipsed Middle English lenvoie (“epilogue”) borrowed ultimately from Old French. Equivalent to epi- + -logue.

s.def: A brief oration or script at the end of a literary piece; an afterword
ex: The novel ended with a short epilogue.

s.def: short speech at the end of a play
A short speech, spoken directly at the audience at the end of a play
ex: In the play’s epilogue, the actor addressed the audience directly.

s.def: The performer who gives this speech
A component of a computer program that prepares the computer to return from a routine.
To conclude with an epilogue.

ety: From Ancient Greek Ἐπιμηθεύς (Epimētheús, “afterthought, hindsight”).

s.def: Son of Iapetus and Clymene, brother to Atlas, Menoetius and Prometheus, of whom he ignored warnings to beware of any gifts from Zeus. He accepted Pandora as his wife, thereby bringing sorrow to the world; father to Pyrrha.
A moon of the planet Saturn.

ety: From Middle English epiphanie, from Old French epyphanie, from Late Latin epiphania, from Ancient Greek ἐπιφάνεια (epipháneia, “manifestation, striking appearance”), from ἐπιφαίνω (epiphaínō, “I appear, display”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “I shine, appear”). English Epiphany (of Christ) since the 14th century, generic use since the 17th century.

s.def: An illuminating realization or discovery, often resulting in a personal feeling of elation, awe, or wonder.
ex: It came to her in an epiphany what her life's work was to be.

s.def: A manifestation or appearance of a divine or superhuman being.
Alternative letter-case form of Epiphany.

s.def: An activity, process, or state that is the result of another; a by-product, a consequence.
A mental process or state that is an incidental by-product of physiological events in the brain or nervous system.
A symptom that develops during the course of a disease that is not connected to the disease.
ex: In all cases, the presence of bile in the blood is a mere epiphænomenon, and therefore demands no special attention.

ety: From epi- + -physis.

s.def: The pineal gland.
The rounded end of any long bone.
A small upper piece of each half of an alveolus of a sea urchin.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐπιφύτον (epiphúton, “one [plant] that grows upon another plant”), from ἐπί (epí, “on top of”) + φυτόν (phutón, “plant”), via epi- (“above, over”) + -phyte (“plant”).

s.def: A plant that grows on another, using it for physical support but obtaining no nutrients from it and neither causing damage nor offering benefit.
ex: The nature of the surface of a plant also determines the number and sort of Epiphytes which lodge on it.

s.def: A fungus that grows on a plant but does not feed upon it saprotrophically (an epiphytic fungus). (The science of detecting and studying any such symbiosis as may be involved in this relationship is still developing.)

s.def: Of or pertaining to an epiphyte.
ex: Near-synonym: holoepiphytic

ety: From Latin Ēpīrus, from Ancient Greek Ἤπειρος (Ḗpeiros, “mainland”).

s.def: A historical region and ancient kingdom in Southeastern Europe, today split politically between northwestern Greece and southwestern Albania.
one of the 13 peripheries
A geographic region and administrative region in northwest Greece, one of the thirteen peripheries of modern Greece.

ety: From episcop (ate) + -acy and/or episcopa(l) + -cy.

s.def: The office of bishop and the governance of a church (a religious denomination) by bishops.
ex: Near-synonyms: bishopric, bishopry, bishopdom, bishopship, bishophood, archbishopric, archbishopry, archbishopdom, archbishopship, archbishophood

s.def: Bishops collectively: Synonym of episcopate.
ex: Near-synonyms: bishopric, bishopry, bishopdom, bishopship, archbishopric, archbishopry, archbishopdom, archbishopship

ety: From Middle English episcopal, from Late Latin episcopālis, from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “watchman, overseer”).

s.def: Of or relating to the affairs of a bishop in various Christian churches.

ety: From Late Latin episcopatus, from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “watching over”).

s.def: Bishops seen as a group.
ex: The American Roman Catholic episcopate meets regularly.

s.def: The tenure in office of a bishop.
ex: Bishop Smith's episcopate ran for more than 30 years.

s.def: A bishop's jurisdiction, the extent of his diocese.
To act as a bishop.

ety: From episio- + -tomy (“surgical incision”), from Ancient Greek ἐπίσιον (epísion, “pubic region”) + τέμνω (témnō, “I cut”)).

s.def: A surgical incision through the perineum made to enlarge the vagina and assist childbirth.
ex: The following eight hours were the worst of my life that haven't ended in an episiotomy.

ety: From French épisode, from New Latin *epīsodium, from Ancient Greek ἐπεισόδιον (epeisódion, “a parenthetic addition, episode”), neuter of ἐπεισόδιος (epeisódios, “following upon the entrance, coming in besides, adventitious”), from ἐπί (epí, “on”) + εἰς (eis, “into”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way”).

s.def: A discrete but connected event, situation, or period within a broader sequence, narrative, or life course.
ex: It was a most embarrassing episode in my life.
Three of the great extinctions appear to have occurred during cold episodes and two during hot episodes.

s.def: A bounded narrative unit within a television series, constituting a single installment that is structurally discrete yet interrelated with the series as a whole.
ex: I can't wait till next week’s episode.

ety: From episode + -ic. Compare French épisodique.

s.def: Relating to an episode.
ex: When I'm not honing my craft in episodic television, I do double-duty as a voice coach.

s.def: Sporadic, happening infrequently and irregularly.
ex: Fortunately, my episodic bouts of dizziness didn't prevent me from climbing Chichen Itzá.

s.def: Consisting of a sequence of seemingly unconnected episodes.
ex: I just read five attempts at episodic novels — has nobody heard of a plot anymore?

s.def: Causing blisters; vesicant.
A vesicant agent; that which causes blisters.
A blister.

ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπίστασις (epístasis, “stopping”), from ἐφίστημι (ephístēmi, “stop”), from ἐφ- (eph-) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “make to stand”). The use in genetics was coined by English biologist William Bateson in 1909 in his book Mendel's Principles of Heredity.

s.def: The modification of the expression of a gene by another unrelated one.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐπίσταξις (epístaxis, “nosebleed”): ἐπί (epí, “above, over, on, upon, besides”) + στάζω (stázō, “to drip (from the nostrils)”).

s.def: Nosebleed.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐπιστήμη (epistḗmē, “science, knowledge”), from ἐπίσταμαι (epístamai, “to know”) + -λογία (-logía, “study or logic of”), from λόγος (lógos, “speech, language”). The term was introduced into English by Scottish philosopher James Frederick Ferrier (1808–1864).

s.def: The branch of philosophy dealing with the study of knowledge; the theory of knowledge, asking such questions as "What is knowledge?", "How is knowledge acquired?", "What do people know?", "How do we know what we know?", "How do we know it is true?", and so on.
A particular instance, version, or school thereof; a particular theory of knowledge.
ex: In his epistemology, Plato maintains that our knowledge of universal concepts is a kind of recollection.

A letter, especially one which is formal or issued publicly.
ex: Wide flew the doors, and lo, / Messire de Beringhen, and this epistle!

s.def: One of the books of the New Testament which was originally a letter issued by an apostle to an individual or a community.
An extract from a New Testament epistle (noun sense 3.1) or book other than a gospel which is read during a church service, chiefly the Eucharist.
To write (something) in, or in the form of, a letter.
To write a letter to (someone).
To write a letter.
To communicate with someone through a letter.
To write (something) as an introduction or preface to a literary work; also, to provide (a literary work) with an introduction or preface.

ety: 1627, from Latin epistolārius, from epistola (“letter”) (English epistle) + -ārius, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ) from ἐπιστέλλω (epistéllō, “to send a message”) from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to prepare, send”). For the noun, compare Middle English pistelarie and Old English pistelari, both from Medieval Latin epistolārium, possibly via an unattested *epistelari, *epistolarie.

s.def: Of or relating to letters, or the writing of letters.
Carried on by written correspondence.
ex: an epistolary relationship

s.def: In the manner of written correspondence.
ex: epistolary style
an epistolary novel
Bram Stoker's novel Dracula (1897) is written in epistolary style.

s.def: A Christian liturgical book containing set readings for church services from the New Testament Epistles.

ety: Latin epistylium, Ancient Greek: compare French épistyle.

s.def: A massive piece of stone or wood laid immediately on the abacus of the capital of a column or pillar; an architrave.

ety: From epi- + syllogism.

s.def: A syllogism which assumes as one of its premises a proposition which was the conclusion of a preceding syllogism (the prosyllogism).

ety: From Old French epitafe, from Late Latin epitaphium (“eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιτάφιος (epitáphios, “relating to a funeral”), from ἐπί (epí, “over”) + τάφος (táphos, “tomb”). By surface analysis epi- + -taph.

s.def: An inscription on a gravestone in memory of the deceased.
A poem or other short text written in memory of a deceased person.
To write or speak after the manner of an epitaph.
ex: The Commons in their speeches epitaph upon him […] "He lived as a wolf and died as a dog."

s.def: To commemorate by an epitaph.
ex: Let me rather be epitaphed the inventor of the English Hexameter.

A song in praise of the bride or bridegroom

s.def: A membranous tissue composed of one or more layers of cells which forms the covering of most internal and external surfaces of the body and its organs: internally including the lining of vessels and other small cavities, and externally being the skin.
ex: The sap of this species was able to cause loss of corneal epithelium 16 h after direct exposure to the sap in a 60-year-old male.

s.def: A term used to characterize a person or thing.
ex: She would lean her head for hours on Beatrice's shoulder, only now and then applying to her some childish and endearing epithet.

s.def: A term used as a qualifier of the name of a deity in order to designate said deity in a particular aspect or role.
A term used as a descriptive substitute for the name or title of a person.
One of many formulaic words or phrases used in the Iliad and Odyssey to characterize a person, a group of people, or a thing.
An abusive or contemptuous word or phrase.
ex: Part of this process was the elaboration of new terms for the Jew, especially the increasingly popular epithet “kike”.
Counterprotesters shouted epithets as they walked by, but the opposing groups kept it nonviolent.
Politico reported that epithets appeared more than 251 times.

s.def: A word in the scientific name of a taxon following the name of the genus or species. This applies only to formal names of plants, fungi and bacteria. In formal names of animals the corresponding term is the specific name.
To term; to refer to as.
ex: He was epitheted "the king of fools".

ety: From Middle French, from Latin epitomē, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτομή (epitomḗ, “an abridgment, also a surface-incision”), from ἐπιτέμνω (epitémnō, “to cut upon the surface, cut short, abridge”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “up”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).

s.def: The embodiment or encapsulation of a class of items.
A representative example.
ex: The minute they see me, fear me / I'm the epitome of "public enemy"
Every single relationship in his life is transactional. That is incredibly pathetic and sad. That is the epitome of a loser.

s.def: The height; the best; the most vivid.
ex: He looks the very epitome of fright: I do not think he could eat one of those apples, if it were given him.

s.def: A brief summary of a text.

ety: Etymology tree English epitome Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English epitomize From epitome + -ize.

s.def: To make an epitome of; to shorten; to condense.
ex: This simple formula epitomizes the kind of 'tolerance' that Marcuse advocates.

s.def: To be an epitome of.
ex: The framework of Combinatory Categorial Grammar epitomizes the rule-based generalized categorial architecture.

ety: From French épizootique, animal equivalent of epidemic, from épizootie, irregularly formed from Ancient Greek ἐπί (epí) + ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”). By surface analysis, epi- + zo- + -otic. Use of the word in the second sense, "an ailment", was likely originally a reference to a particular epizootic ailment. Both senses are attested since at least the 1800s, and the pronunciation with five syllables is explicitly attested since then as well. Dialectal pronunciation of the second sense with four sy…

s.def: An occurrence of a disease or disorder in a population of non-human animals at a frequency higher than that expected in a given time period.
ex: At the same time as an epidemic of the flu broke out among the people, an epizootic of the swine flu broke out among their pigs.

s.def: A particular epizootic disease.
A disease or ailment (of humans).
ex: Johnny's not doing so well today, I think he caught the epizootic.
Never do I have colds — but I got the epizootics(?) and sneezed my head off — twenty three times yesterday.
"My Laws, Minnie! She's got spots! I guess you've got the epizootics."

s.def: Like or having to do with an epizootic: a widespread outbreak of disease among nonhuman animals.
ex: Epizootic plague occurred in the mice following introduction of rats from Europe.
As much attention is being drawn to the subject of epizootic abortion in bovines, [...]

s.def: Containing fossils.
Relating to epizoa; epizoic.

ety: From Medieval Latin epocha, from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ, “a check, cessation, stop, pause, epoch of a star, i.e., the point at which it seems to halt after reaching the highest, and generally the place of a star; hence, a historical epoch”), from ἐπέχω (epékhō, “to hold in, check”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) + ἔχω (ékhō, “to have, hold”). Doublet of epoche.

s.def: A particular period of history, or of a person's life, especially one considered noteworthy or remarkable.
A notable event which marks the beginning of such a period.
A specific instant in time, chosen as the point of reference or zero value of a system that involves identifying instants of time.
ex: UNIX epoch; J2000 epoch

s.def: A geochronologic unit of hundreds of thousands to millions of years; a subdivision of a period, and subdivided into ages (or sometimes subepochs).
One complete presentation of the training data set to an iterative machine learning algorithm.
ex: The neural network was trained over 500 epochs.
For now, let's test and evaluate our GAN by comparing the results from the first epoch with the generated images from the last epoch.

s.def: To divide (data) into segments by time period.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐπῳδός (epōidós); see epi-, ode.

s.def: The after song; the part of a lyric or choral ode which follows the strophe and antistrophe.
A kind of lyric poem, invented by Archilochus, in which a longer verse is followed by a shorter one.

ety: From Latin eponymus, from Ancient Greek ἐπώνῠμος (epṓnŭmos), from ἐπί (epí, “upon, epi-”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”) + -ος (-os, suffix forming adjectives and nouns). Equivalent to epi- + -nym.

s.def: person's name that has given rise to the name of something
A person who gave or supposedly gave their name to a people, place, institution, etc.
Something that is named after a person.
A name taken from a person, a namesake toponym, term, etc.
ex: Alexandria is an eponym, taken from its founder Alexander the Great.
[Mesmer] lives on today as the root of the eponym mesmerize.
For their dubious contribution to literature, Doctor Bowdler and Henrietta were recognized with the eponym bowdlerize[.]

s.def: A name or term derived from any proper noun, inclusive of places, brands, etc.
Synonym of epitome, a person taken as a symbol or quintessential representative of some trait, school, etc.
ex: Rockefeller became the very eponym of wealth.

s.def: Synonym of epithet, a distinguishing title.
ex: It was only posthumously that Julian was distinguished with the eponym "Apostate".

ety: PIE word *h₁epi From Ancient Greek ἐπώνῠμος (epṓnŭmos, “concerning giving one’s name to something; named in a significant manner; surnamed”) + English -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, denoting pertinence or relation).

s.def: Of, relating to, or being the person or entity after which someone or something is named; serving as an eponym.
ex: Prince Hamlet is the eponymous protagonist of the Shakespearian tragedy Hamlet.
Robinson Crusoe is the eponymous hero of the book.
The language Limburgish is named after the eponymous provinces in Belgium and the Netherlands.

s.def: Of a thing: named after a person or entity.
ex: The American singer-songwriter Madonna released her eponymous album in 1983.

ety: Borrowed from French épopée.

s.def: an epic, saga

ety: From Latin epos, from Ancient Greek ἔπος (épos, “word, song, epic”).

s.def: An epic.
The tuber of any one of several edible species of Perideridia spp.

ety: Etymology tree English ep- Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ-der.? Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús) Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁os Proto-Hellenic *génos Ancient Greek γένος (génos) French oxygènebor. English oxygen English -oxy English epoxy From ep- + -oxy.

s.def: Derived from an epoxide.
A thermosetting polyepoxide resin used chiefly in strong adhesives, coatings and laminates; epoxy resin.
To glue with epoxy.
Any of a class of polyether resins, used for coatings, adhesives, and foam.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἒ ψιλόν (è psilón, “simple Ε”).

s.def: The fifth letter of the Greek alphabet, ε or Ε, preceded by delta (Δ, δ) and followed by zeta (Ζ, ζ).
In IPA, the phonetic symbol ɛ that represents the open-mid front unrounded vowel.
An arbitrarily small quantity.
Something negligible or insignificant.
ex: Yes, we have to convert all the symbol names to upper case at startup, but that’s epsilon.
All right, okay. My interest is epsilon.

s.def: The percentage change in an option value with respect to the underlying dividend yield.

ety: Borrowed from German Epstein. See also Epshteyn from Yiddish.

s.def: A surname from German, notably borne by American-British sculptor Jacob Epstein and American sex offender and financier Jeffrey Epstein; variant form Eppstein.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin aequābilis, from aequō (“make level”), from aequus (“even, level”).

s.def: Unvarying, calm and steady; constant and uniform.
ex: The cheerful influence of the morning seemed to have some effect, even upon his equable temper.
Turning to the prisoner, "Budd," he said, and scarce in equable tones, "Budd, if you have aught further to say for yourself, say it now."

s.def: Free from extremes of heat or cold.
Not easily disturbed; tranquil.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *aikʷos? Old Latin aiquos Latin aequus Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālis Latin aequālisbor. Middle English equal English equal From Middle English equal, from Latin aequālis. Doublet of aequalis and egal.

s.def: The same in one or more respects.
ex: Near-synonyms: equivalent; see also Thesaurus:equal

s.def: To be equal to, to have the same value as; to correspond to.
ex: Two plus two equals four.

s.def: A person or thing of equal status to others.
ex: We're all equals here.
This beer has no equal.
Those who were once his equals envy and defame him.

s.def: Fair, impartial.
ex: Are not my ways equal?

s.def: Adequate; sufficiently capable or qualified.
ex: This test is pretty tough, but I think I'm equal to it.
be equal to the task
her comprehension was certainly more equal to the covert meaning, the superior intelligence, of those five letters so arranged.

s.def: Not variable; equable; uniform; even.
ex: an equal movement
an equal temper

s.def: Intended for voices of one kind only, either all male or all female; not mixed.
To make equivalent to; to cause to match.
ex: David equaled the water levels of the bottles, so they now both contain exactly 1 liter.

s.def: To match in degree or some other quality, to match up to.
To have as consequence, to amount to, to mean.
ex: Losing this deal equals losing your job.
Might does not equal right.

s.def: A symbol (=) used in mathematics to indicate that two values are the same, and elsewhere in various other ways, such as (formerly) to separate the signature from the content of a telegram.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French equalité (modern French égalité), from Latin aequālitās, aequālitātem. Doublet of equity. By surface analysis, equal + -ity

s.def: The fact of being equal.
ex: The most powerful of these general ideas which have shaped political development in recent times is of course the ideal of material equality.

s.def: The equal treatment of people irrespective of social or cultural differences.
ex: Jefferson was talking about the equality of natural human rights. You have freedom, and I have freedom. You and I have equal rights to freedom.

s.def: The fact of being equal, of having the same value.

Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English equalize From equal + -ize.

s.def: To make equal; to cause to correspond in amount or degree.
ex: to equalize accounts, burdens, or taxes
One poor moment can suffice / To equalize the lofty and the low.
No system of instruction will completely equalize natural powers.

s.def: To be equal to; to equal, to rival.
ex: polling the reformed churches whether they equalize in number those of his three kingdoms

s.def: To make the scoreline equal by scoring points.
To clear the ears to balance the pressure in the middle ear with the outside pressure by letting air enter along the Eustachian tubes.
to precompose with each of a parallel pair of morphisms so as to yield the same composite morphism.
To adjust the balance between frequency components within an electronic signal.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *aikʷos? Old Latin aiquos Latin aequus Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? s.def: In an equal manner; in equal shares or proportion; with equal and impartial justice; evenly
ex: All citizens are equally taxed.
The pie was divided equally among the guests.
They shared equally in the spoils.

s.def: In equal degree or extent; just as.
ex: The gas stations are equally far from the highway.

s.def: Used to link two or more coordinate elements
ex: John suffered setbacks at his job. Equally, Frank's business slowed.

ety: From French équanimité, from Latin aequanimitās (“calmness, equanimity”), from aequus (“even; calm; fair”) + animus (“mind, soul”) + -itās. By surface analysis, equ- + anim(us) + -ity.

s.def: The state of being calm, stable and composed, especially under stress.
ex: Few people are capable of expressing with equanimity opinions which differ from the prejudices of their social environment.

ety: From Middle English equaten, from Latin aequātus, perfect passive participle of aequō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

ex: Coordinate term: correspond

A statement in assembly language that defines a symbol having a particular value.
ex: The first section of the program includes the system equates.
The following equates define the stats byte […]

ety: From Old French, from Latin aequātiō (“an equalizing”). Morphologically equate + -ion

s.def: An assertion that two expressions are equal, expressed by writing the two expressions separated by an equal sign; in mathematical problems, equations describe various essential aspects of the problem, each of which contributes to the resolution of the problem in part.
The act or process of equating two or more things, or the state of those things being equal (that is, identical).
ex: We need to bring the balance of power into equation

s.def: A small correction to observed values to remove the effects of systematic errors in an observation.

ety: From Late Latin (circulus) aequator (diei et noctis).

s.def: An imaginary great circle around Earth, equidistant from the two poles, and dividing earth's surface into the northern and southern hemispheres.
ex: Baishui is about as close to the equator as Tampa, Florida.

s.def: A similar great circle on any sphere, especially on a celestial body, or on another reasonably symmetrical three-dimensional body.
The midline of any generally spherical object, such as a fruit or vegetable, that has identifiable poles.
ex: Slice the onion through the equator.

s.def: The celestial equator.
Of, near, or relating to the equator.
ex: That plant is best suited to equatorial climates.
In equatorial Ecuador, days and nights are almost the same length, and the sun goes down early.

s.def: Relating to the midline of any approximately spherical object.
of a bond, lying approximately in the plane of a ring, perpendicular to its axis

A kind of telescope mounted so as to have two axes of motion at right angles to each other, one of them parallel to the axis of the Earth, and each carrying a graduated circle, one for measuring declination, and the other right ascension, or the hour angle, so that the telescope may be directed, ev…
A country in Central Africa. Official name: Republic of Equatorial Guinea. Capital: Ciudad de la Paz.

ety: From an alteration of earlier esquiry (through the influence of the unrelated Latin equus), from Middle French escuirie, escuerie, derivative of escuyer (“squire”), or alternatively from Medieval Latin scuria (“stable”), from Old High German scura (“barn”). Compare esquire.

s.def: An officer responsible for the care and supervision of the horses of a person of rank.
A personal attendant to a head of state, a member of a royal family, or a national representative.

ety: Ultimately from Latin equester (“of or pertaining to equestrians/cavalry”) + -ianus (“-ian, related to”, adjective marker), from equus (“horse”).

s.def: Of horseback riding or horseback riders.
ex: They were an equestrian people.
After his death an equestrian statue was erected.

s.def: Of or relating to the ancient Roman class of equites.
One who rides a horse.
Synonym of eques.

s.def: The art or sport of horseriding; the skill required for it.

Describing a map projection that preserves scale. No map can show scale correctly throughout the entire map but some can show true scale between one or two points and every point or along every meridian and these are referred to as equidistant.

Occupying a position that is an equal distance between several points. ex: Kissinger had wanted to keep an “equilateral” distance between the US, USSR and China. Under Carter, they became de facto partners.

s.def: Having all the faces equal.
Having the two sides equal, as a surface divisible by a longitudinal median line into two halves of the same form.
Having all the convolutions of the shell in one plane, chiefly of foraminifers.
A side exactly corresponding, or equal, to others.
A figure having all its sides equal.
A force equal to, but opposite of, the resultant sum of vector forces; that force which balances other forces, thus bringing an object to equilibrium.

ety: From the participle stem of Late Latin *aequilībrō.

s.def: To balance, or bring into equilibrium.
ex: Their equilibrium level is due to both trend inflation and r#42;, the real neutral rate of interest that equilibrates the economy in the long run.

s.def: To balance, to be in a state of equilibrium.

ety: First attested in the mid 18th century. From French équilibriste, from équilibre (“balance”).

s.def: A tightrope walker.

ety: From Latin aequilībrium, from equal + lībra (“balance”).

s.def: The condition of a system in which competing influences are balanced, resulting in no net change.
Mental balance.
ex: Tiffany Pollard: What just happened?! Eric Andre: That coffee mug is broken. Tiffany Pollard: I can't take this. This is gonna mess up my equilibrium.

s.def: The state of a reaction in which the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are the same.
The state of a body at rest or in uniform motion in which the resultant of all forces on it is zero.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin equīnus (“of or pertaining to horses”).

s.def: Of, relating to, or reminiscent of horses.
ex: The equine escapees caused chaos bolting through the capital, colliding with vehicles and startling pedestrians.

s.def: Of or relating to any member or members of the genus Equus, including horses, donkeys, mules, zebras, and others.
Any horse or horse-like animal, especially one of the genus Equus.

ety: Inherited from Middle English equinoctial, equinoccial, equinoxial, from Old French equinoxial, from Latin (circulus) aequinoctiālis, from aequinoctium + -alis.

s.def: Of or relating to the spring or autumnal equinox.
ex: an equinoctial gale or storm, i.e. one happening at or near the time of the equinox, in any part of the world

s.def: Of or relating to the celestial equator.

Of flowers: that open and close at particular times of day.
The great circle midway between the celestial poles; the celestial equator.
The terrestrial equator.
An equinoctial gale.
ex: Heavy with storm the coast-lines grew, / And sharp the equinoctials blew

ety: PIE word *nókʷts From Middle English equinox, equinoxe, equynox (“one of the two periods in the year when the day and night are of equal length, equinox; either the zodiac sign Aries or Libra, in which the sun crosses the celestial equator”), from Old French equinoce, equinoxe (modern French équinoxe), or from its etymon Medieval Latin ēquinoxium, ēquinoctium, from Latin aequinoctium (“equinox”), from aequus (“equal”) + nox (“night”) (ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts (“night”…

s.def: one of the two times in the year when the length of the day and night are equal, which occurs when the apparent path of the Sun intersects with the equatorial plane of the Earth

One of two times in the year (one in March and the other in September) when the length of the day and the night are equal, which occurs when the sun is directly overhead at the equator; this marks the beginning of spring in one hemisphere and autumn in the other.
The circumstance of a twenty-four hour time period having the day and night of equal length.
One of the two points in space where the apparent path of the Sun intersects with the equatorial plane of the Earth.
A gale (“very strong wind”) once thought to occur more frequently around the time of an equinox (sense 1), now known to be a misconception; an equinoctial gale.
ex: The Equinox drove the sand into their faces or round their legs, as they dived among the sheep-haunted hollows.

s.def: A celestial equator (“great circle on the celestial sphere, coincident with the plane of the Earth's equator (the equatorial plane)”); also, the Earth's equator.

ety: From French équiper (“to supply, fit out”), originally said of a ship, Old French esquiper (“to embark”); of Germanic origin, most probably from Old Norse skipa (“to man (a ship)”), from Proto-Germanic *skipōną (“to ship, sail, embark”). Compare with Middle High German schipfen, German schiffern, Icelandic skipa, Old English scipian. Doublet of ship.

s.def: To supply with something necessary in order to carry out a specific action or task; to provide with (e.g. weapons, provisions, munitions, rigging).
ex: 1698-1699, Edmund Ludlow, Memoirs Gave orders for equipping a considerable fleet.

s.def: To dress up; to array; to clothe.
ex: The country are led astray in following the town, and equipped in a ridiculous habit, when they fancy themselves in the height of the mode.

s.def: To prepare (someone) with a skill.
ex: I'm sorry, but I don't feel equipped to answer that kinda question yet.
it is no more than proper that you should equip us with a vessel in which to pursue the journey which you interrupted

s.def: To equip oneself with (an item); to bring (equipment) into active use.
ex: Take it down from a distance with a magic spell, or equip your sword and attack it at close range.

s.def: Equipment (carried by a game character).

ety: From Middle French equippage, from equipper. The "carriage" sense may be influenced by Latin equus (“horse”).

s.def: Equipment or supplies, especially military ones.
A type of horse-drawn carriage.
The carriage together with attendants; a retinue.
Military dress; uniform, armour, etc.
ex: Loe-heere a description, much resembling the equipage of a compleat French-man at armes, with all his bards.

s.def: To furnish with an equipage.

ety: From equip + -ment, or from French équipement.

s.def: The act of equipping, or the state of being equipped, as for a voyage or expedition.
Any items used in equipping something or someone, for example things needed for an expedition or voyage.
ex: We need more gardening equipment if we want to properly landscape our yard, not just a rake and some gloves.
The sports shop sells different kits of famous clubs, and equipment from all kind of sports.
Armed and dight, In the equipments of a knight.

s.def: The male genitalia.

s.def: A state of balance; equilibrium.
ex: Government was unnerved, confounded, and in a manner suspended. Its equipoise was totally gone.
“An easy evasion”, retorted the excited bride, who had lost her mental equipoise.
The words were not without emotion, and retained their level tone as if by a careful equipoise between imminent extremes.

s.def: A counterbalance.
ex: Perhaps that quality which existed, in spite of the equipoise against it, in Sir Howard, was fidelity in friendship.
The cone's not fixed, it's hung by a chain from a lever, and balanced by an equipoise.
Her smiling equipoise is a statement of self-confident power against his sour fuming.

s.def: To act or make to act as an equipoise.
To cause to be or stay in equipoise.

ety: From French équipollent, from Latin aequipollēns.

able to be deduced from the other
equivalent
An equivalent.

ex: When the two arms of a lever and the power are given, to find the weight that will equiponderate […]

s.def: A counterbalance.

ex: The random number generator is designed to generate random numbers with an equiprobable law of distribution with the limits +1 to -1.

ety: From Latin equus (“horse”) + saeta (“bristle”).

s.def: A horsetail (plant of genus Equisetum)

ety: From French équitable, from Old French, from equité (“equity”).

s.def: Fair, just, or impartial.
ex: I may justly require you to produce that argument; nor have you any pretence to refuse so equitable a demand.
Security can be obtained but by defined rights, and these can be ensured only by equitable laws.

s.def: Marked by or having equity.
Relating to the general principles of justice that correct or supplement the provisions of the law; relating to equity or courts of equity.

ety: From French équitation.

s.def: The art, practice or act of horseriding.

ety: From Middle English equitee, equytee, from Old French equité, from Latin aequitās (“uniformity; impartiality; fairness”).

s.def: Fairness, impartiality, or justice as determined in light of "natural law" or "natural right".
ex: “One of the staff said, ‘That’s fine, Delia. But what do wolves have to do with equity, justice and inclusion?’" Ms. Malone said.

s.def: Various related senses originating with the Court of Chancery in late Medieval England
ex: 1800, Lloyd Kenyon, 1st Baron Kenyon in Mayor, &c. of Southampton v. Graves (1800), 8 T. R. 592. A Court of equity knows its own province.
A Court of equity interposes only according to conscience.

s.def: Various senses related to net value
ex: I have a lot of equity in my house.

s.def: Equality
ex: What steps the Government are taking to help ensure equity of opportunity for people from low-income families.

ety: From Latin aequivalentem, accusative singular of aequivalēns, present active participle of aequivaleō (“to be equivalent, have equal power”). By surface analysis, equi- + -valent. Mostly displaced native Middle English efenmete (See evenmete).

s.def: Containing an error; inaccurate.
ex: His answer to the sum was erroneous.
An erroneous early Fox News report about the New Orleans terror attack is warping the political dialogue in the aftermath of the deadly rampage.

s.def: Derived from an error.
ex: His conclusion was erroneous, since it was based on a false assumption.

s.def: Mistaken.
ex: Her choice at the line-up proved to be erroneous, as she had only seen the mugger for an instant.

s.def: Wandering; erratic.
Deviating from the requirements of the law, but without a lack of legal authority, thus not illegal.
ex: If, while having the power to act, one commits error in the exercise of that power, he acts erroneously.

ety: From Middle English errour, from Anglo-Norman errour, borrowed from Old French error, from Latin error (“wandering about”, noun), derived from the verb errō (“to wander, to err”). Cognate with Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌶𐌴𐌹 (airzei, “error”), Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌶𐌾𐌰𐌽 (airzjan, “to lead astray”). More at err. By surface analysis, err + -or (suffix forming nouns of quality, state, or condition). Displaced native Old English dwild (“error”).

s.def: mistake — see also mistake
The state, quality, or condition of being wrong.
ex: "Am I in error in marking out the s in the word assistants used in the following manner?[…]"

s.def: A mistake; an accidental wrong action or a false statement not made deliberately.
ex: There was a large error in the accounts.
Chris Brunt sliced the spot-kick well wide but his error was soon forgotten as Olsson headed home from a corner.

s.def: Sin; transgression.
ex: I've finally seen the error of my ways.

s.def: A failure to complete a task, usually involving a premature termination.
The difference between a measured or calculated value and a true one.
A play which is scored as having been made incorrectly.
One or more mistakes in a trial that could be grounds for review of the judgement.
Any alteration in the DNA chemical structure occurring during DNA replication, recombination or repairing.
An unintentional deviation from the inherent rules of a language variety made by a second language learner.
A message displayed when a failure condition occurs, usually on a computer or device.

ety: From error + -free.

s.def: Free from errors.
ex: The realization of the interior orientation is assumed as errorfree.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ud-s-? Proto-Indo-European *h₂u-s-? Proto-Germanic *uz- Proto-West Germanic *uʀ- Proto-Indo-European *sed- Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éyeti Proto-Indo-European *sodéyeti Proto-Germanic *satjaną Proto-West Germanic *sattjan Proto-West Germanic *uʀsattjan Old High German irsezzen Middle High German ersetzen German ersetzenbf. German Ersatzbor. English ersatz Borrowed from German Ersatz (“replacement, substitute”), a back-formation from ers…

s.def: An inauthentic or inadequate substitute or imitation.
ex: Back then, we could only get ersatz coffee.
The crowd wandered out to a huge party on the ersatz city blocks of the Paramount lot.

s.def: Something made in imitation; an effigy or substitute.
ex: They don't have the skills to tell ersatz magic from the real thing, for as children they daily invested the ersatz with what imagination they had.
“You do Berlin a disservice, baron. We too have mastered a few things: ersatzes, for instance, and the metaphysics of fictionalism—”

ety: From Middle English erste, from Old English ǣresta (“first”), from Proto-West Germanic *airist (“earliest, first”), equivalent to ere + -est. Cognate with North Frisian iarst, iáárs, jarst, jest (“first”), West Frisian earst (“first”), Dutch eerste (“first”), German erste (“first”).

s.def: First.
First of all, before (some other specified thing).
Sooner (than); before.
Formerly, once, erstwhile.
ex: When lofty trees I see barren of leaves Which erst from heat did canopy the herd

ety: 18th century. From Latin erubescens, present participle of erubescere (“to grow red”); e (“out”) + rubescere. See rubescent. By surface analysis, e- + Latin rub(eō) + -escent.

s.def: Red; reddish.
ex: Fruits ovoid or orbicular, without nutlets at base, narrow into a neck, often underdeveloped, white, greenish white and erubescent only on 1 side

s.def: Blushing
ex: [T]he Major erubescent confounded the impudence of the young folks, and said when he had his hair cut he would keep a lock of it for Miss Laura.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin ēructātus, from the verb ēructō.

s.def: To belch, to burp.

ety: From Latin ērudītus, participle of ērudiō (“educate, train”), from e- (“out of”) + rudis (“rude, unskilled”). Doublet of erudit.

s.def: Learned, scholarly, with emphasis on knowledge gained from books.
ex: The professor gave an erudite lecture that impressed everyone in the audience.
His erudite knowledge of ancient history made him a sought-after speaker.
She was praised for her erudite contributions to the academic journal.

s.def: a learned or scholarly person

ety: First attested in the 15th Century. From Middle French érudition, from Latin eruditio (“an instructing, learning, erudition”), from erudire (“to instruct, educate, cultivate”, literally “free from rudeness”), from e (“out”) + rudis (“rude”). By surface analysis, erudite + -ion.

s.def: Profound knowledge acquired from learning and scholarship.
The refinement, polish and knowledge that education confers.

ety: From Latin eruptus, past participle of ērumpō (“to break out (of), to burst out (from)”), from e (“out”) + rumpō (“to break”).

s.def: To eject something violently (such as lava or water, as from a volcano or geyser).
ex: The volcano erupted, spewing lava across a wide area.

s.def: To burst forth; to break out.
ex: The third molar tooth erupts late in most people, and sometimes does not appear at all.

s.def: To spontaneously release pressure or tension.
ex: The crowd erupted in anger.
The whole table erupted in laughter.
And Stamford Bridge erupted with joy as Florent Malouda slotted in a cross from Drogba, who had stayed just onside.

s.def: (Of birds, insects, etc.) To suddenly appear in a certain region in large numbers.
ex: After particularly good seasons, flocks "erupt" from their breeding grounds and appear in reed beds where they have not been seen for years, if ever.

ety: From Middle French éruption, from Latin eruptio.

s.def: A violent ejection, such as the spurting out of lava from a volcano.
ex: a volcanic eruption

s.def: A sudden release of pressure or tension.
ex: There was an eruption of joy at the final whistle.

s.def: An utterance, especially a sudden one; an ejaculation.
An infection of the skin resulting in a rash or blemishing.

ety: From French éruptif. By surface analysis, erupt + -ive.

s.def: That erupts or bursts forth.
Accompanied by eruptions.
ex: an eruptive fever

s.def: Produced by eruption.
ex: eruptive rocks, such as the igneous or volcanic
The region is further diversified by short ranges of eruptive mountains.

s.def: An eruptive rock, one produced by eruption.

ety: Ultimately from Latin ēryngion, from Ancient Greek ἠρύγγιον (ērúngion), from ἤρυγγος (ḗrungos).

s.def: The root of sea holly, Eryngium maritimum, formerly candied and taken as confectionery and held to have aphrodisiac properties.
Any other plant of the same genus, Eryngium.

ety: From Middle English erisipila, borrowed from Latin erysipelas, from Ancient Greek ἐρῠσῐ́πελᾰς (erŭsĭ́pelăs), probably related to ἐρῠθρός (erŭthrós, “red”) and πέλμᾰ (pélmă, “the sole of a foot”).

s.def: An acute, sometimes recurrent febrile disease caused by infection of a hemolytic streptococcus, associated with intense edematous local inflammation of the skin and subcutaneous tissues, and marked by large raised red patches on the skin.

ety: From New Latin erythēma, from Ancient Greek ἐρύθημα (erúthēma, “a redness or flush on the skin”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”)..

s.def: Abnormal redness and inflammation of the skin, due to vasodilation.
Skin redness from sunburn or chemical irritation

ety: By surface analysis, erythr- (“red”) + -ism (noun suffix).

s.def: An abnormally red or pink pigmentation found in certain animals.

ety: From erythr- + -ite.

s.def: Red cobalt, a secondary hydrated arsenate of cobalt minerals with the formula (Co₃(AsO₄)₂·8H₂O).

ety: From erythro- (“red”) + -cyte (“cell”), referring to the red color of hemoglobin when oxygen is bound to it.

s.def: A hemoglobin-containing cell, especially as found in humans but more generally present in the blood of most vertebrates, that is involved with the transport of oxygen; such cells are usually anucleate in humans and many other animals.

ety: Etymology tree English (Streptomyces) erythr(eus) Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-)der. Latin -o-bor. English -o- English -mycin English erythromycin From (Streptomyces) erythr(eus) + -o- + -mycin (“antibiotic from a Streptomyces strain”).

s.def: A broad-spectrum macrolide antibiotic C₃₇H₆₇NO₁₃ produced by an actinomycete Saccharopolyspora erythraea (formerly Streptomyces erythreus) and similar in its effects to penicillin, administered orally or topically in the treatment of infections caused by Gram-positive bacteria.
An antibiotic similar to penicillin, used for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἐρυθρός (eruthrós, “red”) and ποιητής (poiētḗs, “creator, maker”) and -in.

s.def: A glycoprotein hormone that functions as a cytokine for erythrocyte precursors in bone marrow.
The ketotetrose (R)-1,3,4-trihydroxybutan-2-one used in some artificial tanning preparations
A municipality, the capital of Erzincan district and Erzincan Province, Turkey.
A province in eastern Turkey.
A district of Erzincan Province, Turkey.
A city, the capital of Erzurum Province, Turkey.
A province and metropolitan municipality in northeastern Turkey.

ety: Borrowed from French escalade, from Italian scalata, from scalare (“to climb”), from scala (“ladder”), from Latin scālae (“ladder”). Doublet of scalade.

s.def: An act of scaling walls or fortifications.
ex: An escalade was required for the warriors to attack the troops.

s.def: To scale the walls of a fortification.

ety: Back-formation from escalator.

s.def: To increase (something) in extent or intensity; to intensify or step up.
ex: Violence escalated during the election.
The shooting escalated the existing hostility.
A small fight escalated into a big fight.

s.def: In technical support, to transfer a customer, a problem, etc. to the next higher level of authority
ex: The tech 1 escalated the caller to a tech 2.

s.def: To climb.
ex: They escalated upstairs to the Mall coffee tables.
James worked through the basics, escalating up the ladder of complex moves.
We were escalating up a few hundred feet into the canyon.

s.def: To move by escalator.
ex: Escalator after escalator flowed up to the heights above, […] Dov escalated up beside me, scowling.
Escalating up the up escalator at Green Park Tube station was a hundred times better than walking up two loads of steps at Oxford Circus.

ety: Etymology tree English escalate Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ātiōlbor. Old French -ationbor. Middle English -acioun English -ation English -ion English escalation From escalate + -ion.

s.def: A deliberate or premeditated increase in the violence or geographic scope of a conflict.
The act of escalating.
An increase or rise, especially to counteract a perceived discrepancy.
The reassignment of a difficult problem to someone whose job is dedicated to handling such cases.
ex: The manager ensures that the escalation team generates a continuous stream of root cause analysis exercises and the subsequent corrective actions.

ety: By genericization from the former trademark Escalator, created by American inventor Charles Seeberger in 1900, from Latin ē- (“from, out of”) + scala (“ladder”) + -tor, which forms nouns of agency; see the appendix. Broader usage may be influenced by its derivative escalate, by surface analysis, escalate + -or. For an alternative etymology, see the Online Etymology Dictionary.

s.def: A motor-driven mechanical device consisting of a continuous loop of steps that automatically conveys people from one floor to another.
ex: There is a plastic molly-guard covering the escalator's shutdown button to prevent little kids from pushing it and stopping the escalator.

s.def: Anything that escalates.
An upward or progressive course.
ex: Lots of people fell for the pitch that real estate was an up-only escalator into the American Dream

s.def: An escalator clause.
ex: They agreed to a cost-of-living escalator.

ety: Borrowed from French escapade (“the act of escaping; a trick”), itself borrowed from Old Spanish escapada, from escapar (“to escape”), from Vulgar Latin *excappāre.

s.def: A daring or adventurous act; an undertaking which goes against convention.

ety: From Middle English escapen, from Anglo-Norman and Old Northern French escaper ( = Old French eschaper, modern French échapper), from Vulgar Latin *excappāre (“to escape a garment, get out of one's clothing”, literally “to free oneself from one's cape”), from Latin ex- (“out”) + Late Latin cappa (“cape, cloak”). Cognate with escapade. Also doublet of scape.

s.def: To get free; to free oneself.
ex: The prisoners escaped by jumping over a wall.
The factory was evacuated after toxic gases escaped from a pipe.

s.def: To avoid (any unpleasant person or thing); to elude, get away from.
ex: He only got a fine and so escaped going to jail.
The children climbed out of the window to escape the fire.
There's no escaping the fact that the house needs painting.

s.def: To avoid capture; to get away with something, avoid punishment.
ex: Luckily, I escaped with only a fine.

s.def: The act of leaving a dangerous or unpleasant situation.
ex: The prisoners made their escape by digging a tunnel.

s.def: To break out of confinement.
ex: The prisoners escaped their cell.

s.def: To avoid responsibilities and stresses for a time.
ex: Work was stressful, and I needed to escape.

s.def: To be forgotten by.
ex: I used to know the name of the capital of France, but it escapes me now.

s.def: To elude the observation or notice of; to not be seen or remembered by.
ex: The name of the hotel escapes me at present.
The detective examined the crime scene, but one clue escaped his notice.
c. 1698-1699 (year published) Edmund Ludlow, Memoirs They escaped the search of the enemy.

s.def: To cause (a single character, or all such characters in a string) to be interpreted literally, instead of with any special meaning it would usually have in the same context, often by prefixing with another character.
ex: When using the "bash" shell, you can escape the ampersand character with a backslash.
Brion escaped the double quote character on Windows by adding a second double quote within the literal.
If the data for a URI component would conflict with the reserved purpose, then the conflicting data must be escaped before forming the URI.

s.def: To halt a program or command by pressing a key (such as the "Esc" key) or combination of keys.

ety: From escape + room.

s.def: A room containing various puzzles and riddles that players must solve in order to escape.
The minimum speed needed to escape the gravitational field of a planet or other body.
ex: The gravitational force exerted by a planet determines its surface gravity and escape velocity.

s.def: A major breakthrough or milestone; momentum.
ex: “All signs point to Netflix having reached escape velocity, with subscribers scaling far faster than investors expected,” Mr. Greenfield said.

ety: Etymology tree English escape Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. English -ism English escapism From escape + -ism.

s.def: An inclination to escape from routine or reality into fantasy.
A genre of book, film etc. that one uses to indulge this tendency.
The performance of an escape artist.

ety: Etymology tree English escape Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Hellenic *-tās Ancient Greek -τής (-tḗs) Ancient Greek -ῐστής (-ĭstḗs)bor. Latin -istader. Old French -istebor. Middle English -ist English -ist English escapist From escape + -ist.

s.def: Intended for or tending toward escape; especially, used to avoid, deny, or forget about reality, as through fantasy.
ex: He enjoys reading escapist fiction in his free time.

s.def: Someone who wants to escape; especially from reality

ety: Borrowed from French escargot.

s.def: A dish, commonly associated with French cuisine, consisting of edible snails.
A snail (often Helix pomatia) used in preparation of that dish.

ety: Borrowed from French escarole, from Italian scariola, scarola (“chicory; endive”), from Late Latin escariola, scariola, from Latin ēsca (“food; dish prepared for the table”) (from edō (“to eat”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed- (“to eat”)) + -ola (from -olus, -ulus (suffix forming diminutive nouns)). Doublet of scariole.

s.def: A subspecies or variety of broad-leaved endive (Cichorium endivia subsp. endivia, syn. Cichorium endivia var. latifolium), which is eaten as a vegetable.
ex: Like chicory and Belgian endive, escarole’s bitterness is its attraction. Look for broad heads of escarole with dark green leaves.

ety: From French escarpe, from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz. Doublet of scarp.

s.def: Obsolete spelling of scarp.
Obsolete spelling of scarp.
ex: Our men, though quite expos'd, and though the Glacis was all escarp'd upon the live Rock, went on with an undaunted Courage

ety: From Middle French eschare (now escarre) or Late Latin eschara (“scar, scab”), from Ancient Greek ἐσχάρα (eskhára, “hearth, brazier, scab”). Doublet of scar.

s.def: A superficial structure of dead tissue, usually hardened, and commonly but not necessarily dark, adhering to underlying living or necrotic tissue, caused by gangrene or a burn.

Any hard, dark, commonly flattened or sunken lesion or crust, especially on a burn, abscess, infection, wound; commonly a coagulation of blood or exudations, not necessarily involving dead or necrotic tissue.
ex: When the caustic is removed, the eschar should be punctured for the discharge of the matter, and then dressed with warm emollient poultices...

s.def: The emotional imprint of a trauma such as grief, loss, or degradation.
ex: In another minute there was no letter; but, as with every other relationship in my life, an eschar of ashes. The word is rare, but exact.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek ἔσχατος (éskhatos) Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *lóǵos Proto-Hellenic *lógos Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos) Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-i-eh₂ Proto-Hellenic *-íā Ancient Greek -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā) Ancient Greek -λογῐ́ᾱ (-logĭ́ā)bor. Latin -logialbor. French -logiebor. English -logy English eschatology From Ancient Greek ἔσχατος (éskhatos, “last”) + English -logy.

s.def: A system of doctrines concerning final matters, such as death.
The study of the end times—the end of the world, notably in Christian and Islamic theology, the second coming of Christ, the Apocalypse, or the Last Judgment.
ex: Eschatology and proleptics aside, I think this is a really stupid way to read a mystery novel.

ety: From Middle English escheat, achete, eschete (“the reversion or conversion of property to the government”), from Anglo-Norman eschete and Old French eschet, escheit, escheoit (“that which falls to one”), past participle of escheoir (“to fall”) (modern French échoir), from Late Latin *excadēre (“fall away, fall out”), from (Latin) ex- + cadere (“fall”). Doublet of cheat.

s.def: The return, conversion, or vesting of property of a deceased person or closed business to the government (originally to a feudal lord) where there are no legal heirs or claimants. It is known as bona vacantia in the United Kingdom.
The property so reverted.
Plunder, booty.
That which falls to one; a reversion or return.
ex: And by my ruines thinkes to make them great: / To make one great by others losse, is bad excheat

s.def: To put (land, property) in escheat; to confiscate.
ex: Failure to perform duties opened the culprit to charges of ‘felony’ (felonia), providing grounds for the king to escheat the fief.

s.def: To revert, convert, or vest ownership to the government or lord because its previous owner died without an heir or a business closed and no one claims the assets.

ety: From Middle English eschewen, from Anglo-Norman eschiver, (third-person present eschiu), from Frankish *skiuhijan (“to dread, shun, avoid”); thus a doublet of skew. For the pronunciation with /ʃ/, compare the development of marshal from Middle English marschal (/marsˈt͡ʃaːl/) or Middle English myssheve, variant of myschef (“hardship”). Variants in /sk/ are either from unattested Middle English *eskewen (from Old Northern French eskiver; compare skew) or are spelling pronunciations. See also Fre…

s.def: To avoid; to shun, to shy away from.
ex: What cannot be eschew'd must be embrac'd.
Let him eschew evil, and do good; let him seek peace, and ensue it.
Above all, let her eschew the impertinence of invention; let her leave genius to her milliner.

ety: From a phonetic spelling of the letter S, with citalopram, since this drug is the (S)-stereoisomer of the earlier drug citalopram.

s.def: A drug that functions as an SSRI and is administered orally in the form of its oxalate C₂₀H₂₁FN₂O·C₂H₂O₄ to treat depression and anxiety.

ety: Borrowed from French escorte, itself borrowed from Italian scorta.

s.def: A group of people or vehicles, generally armed, who go with a person or people of importance to safeguard them on a journey or mission.
An accompanying person in such a group.
A guard who travels with a dangerous person, such as a criminal, for the protection of others.
A group of people attending as a mark of respect or honor.
An accompanying person in a social gathering, etc.
Protection, care, or safeguard on a journey or excursion.
A sex worker who does not operate in a brothel, but with whom clients make appointments; a call girl or male equivalent; a pimp.
ex: Every escort has at least one or two regular clients; they are our bread and butter.

s.def: To attend to in order to guard and protect; to accompany as a safeguard (for the person escorted or for others); to give honorable or ceremonious attendance to.
ex: Lord Lyndsey, ever attentive, escorted his Lady to the carriage

s.def: To accompany (a person) in order to compel them to go somewhere (e.g. to leave a building).
To go with someone as a partner, for example on a formal date.

ety: From French escritoire, from escrire (“to write”) (obsolete forms of écritoire and écrire, respectively) + -oire (“a tool or object”). Doublet of scriptorium.

s.def: A writing desk with a hinged door that provides the writing surface.
ex: Rosemary sat at her Public Works Department escritoire, in a sea of fed cats, and tried to write a letter to Vythilingam.

ety: Learned borrowing from Latin ēsculentus (“fit for eating, eatable, edible; good to eat, delicious; nourishing; full of food”) + English -ent (suffix forming adjectives with the sense of causing, doing, or promoting a certain action). Ēsculentus is derived from ēsca (“food; dish prepared for the table; bait”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed- (“to eat”)) + -ulentus (suffix meaning ‘abounding in, full of’ forming adjectives).

s.def: Suitable for eating; eatable, edible.
ex: Nicolas Venette, French physician, refers to skirret, a plant that has esculent tubers, for its high aphrodisiac potential.
But beyond plants esculent and floral, John Quincey Adams favored trees.

s.def: “Good enough to eat”; attractive.
Something edible, especially a vegetable; a comestible.
ex: Meanwhile, maize and morning glories, tomatoes and cherry trees, every flower and Esculent known to [Carl] Linnæus, thriv'd.

s.def: An edible mushroom.
ex: [Morchella] esculentoides [is] similar to Morchella esculenta, a European esculent, whose name, appropriately, means "edible".

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *sek-? Proto-Indo-European *-éyti Proto-Indo-European *skey-der. Proto-Indo-European *skoy-tó-m Proto-Italic *skoitom? Latin scūtum Old French escutder. Old French escu Proto-Indo-European *-ōder. Proto-Indo-European *-Hōder.? Latin -ō Frankishinflu. Old French -on Anglo-Norman escuchonbor. Middle English scochon English escutcheon From Middle English scochon, from Anglo-Norman escuchon, Old French escusson (French écusson), ultimately from Latin scutum (“shie…

s.def: The shield on which a coat of arms is displayed, or, by extension, the coat of arms itself.
ex: Meronyms: field, charge, emblem

s.def: A small shield used to charge a larger one.
The pattern of distribution of hair upon the pubic mound.
A marking upon the back of a cow's udder and the space above it (the perineum), formed by the hair growing upward or outward instead of downward. It was once taken as an index of milking qualities.
ex: The milk-mirror, or escutcheon, is formed by the hair above the udder, extending upwards between the thighs, […]

s.def: The part of a ship's stern where its name is displayed.
A decorative or protective plate or bezel designed to fill the gap between a switch, pipe, valve, control knob, etc., and the surface from which it protrudes.
The insignia around a doorknob's exterior hardware or a door lock's cosmetic plate.
The depression behind the beak of certain bivalves; the ligamental area.

ety: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish ése (“dude”).

s.def: dude, man. (Usually used vocatively).
Obsolete spelling of ease.

ety: From Irish eiscir (“esker, glacial ridge”).

s.def: A long, narrow, sinuous ridge created by deposits from a stream running beneath a glacier.

ety: Attested since 1584, from French Esquimau, ultimately from an Old Montagnais term. Ives Goddard's theory, accepted by most linguists today, is that it derives from Montagnais ayaškimew (“snowshoe-netter”). An older theory, defended by John Steckley due to its greater acceptance in Native oral traditions, but discredited by linguists, is that it derives from a term meaning "eater(s) of raw meat". Details * The theory most accepted among linguists today is that it derives from ayaškimew (“snowsho…

s.def: member of the Eskimo people(s)
A member of a group of indigenous peoples inhabiting the Arctic, from Siberia, through Alaska and Northern Canada, to Greenland, including the Inuit and Yupik.
A dog of the American Eskimo breed.
ex: Yet many pure-bred, if unregistered, Eskimos are still kept along the Canadian border for use in sled racing.

s.def: A dog of the Canadian Eskimo breed.
A team member of the Canadian Football League's Edmonton Eskimos. (Obsolete as of 2020 with the team dropping this name in favour of Elks in 2021.)
Any of the languages of the Eskimo people.

ety: So called after an Inuit traditional greeting or sign of affection, the *kunik, in which the nose and upper lip are placed against another's skin while breathing in.

s.def: The rubbing of one's nose against another's as a sign of affection.

ety: From Turkish Eskişehir, from Ottoman Turkish اسكی شهر (Eski Şehir, “Old Town”).

s.def: A city in Turkey.
A province of Turkey.

ety: From esophag- + -itis.

s.def: An inflammation of the oesophagus.

ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐσωτερικός (esōterikós, “belonging to an inner circle”), from ἐσωτέρω (esōtérō, “further inside”), comparative of ἔσω (ésō, “within”), from ἐς (es), εἰς (eis, “into”) (the term esoteric referred originally to the secret teachings of Greek philosophers, versus public or exoteric ones).

s.def: Confidential; private.

an esoteric meeting

Describing the thermodynamic equilibrium conditions where a liquid coexists with two solid phases.
A material that has the composition of a eutectic mixture or eutectic alloy.
The temperature of the eutectic point.

ety: First attested in 1606, from Ancient Greek εὐθανασία (euthanasía), from εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + θάνατος (thánatos, “death”)

s.def: The practice of killing a human being who is considered a liability to society, especially a disabled person.

ex: For myself I could hold it in my account with God to find such an euthanasia for you, even at this moment if it were best.

ety: First attested in 1526; borrowed from Latin ēvacuātus, the perfect passive participle of ēvacuō (“to empty out, evacuate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

s.def: To leave or withdraw from; to quit; to retire from.
ex: The soldiers evacuated the fortress.
The firefighters told us to evacuate the area as the flames approached.
The Norwegians were forced to evacuate the country.

s.def: To cause (or help) to leave or withdraw from.
ex: The firefighters decided to evacuate all the inhabitants from the street.

s.def: To make empty; to empty out; to remove the contents of, including to create a vacuum.
ex: The scientist evacuated the chamber before filling it with nitrogen.

s.def: To make empty; to deprive.
ex: Evacuate the Scriptures of their most important doctrines.

s.def: To remove; to eject; to void; to discharge, as the contents of a vessel, or of the bladder or the bowels (to stool).

it would not evacuate a marriage after cohabitation and actual consummation

ety: From Middle English evacuacioun, from Old French evacuation, from Late Latin ēvacuātiō. Equivalent to evacuate + -ion.

The act of emptying, clearing of the contents, or discharging, including creating a vacuum.

Voidance of any matter by the natural passages of the body or by an artificial opening; defecation; urination; also, a diminution of the fluids of an animal body by cathartics, venesection, or other means.
That which is evacuated or discharged; especially, a discharge by stool, urine or other natural means.
Abolition; nullification.

ety: From French évacué, évacuée, from évacuer, equivalent to evacu(ate) + -ee.

ety: From Middle French évader, from Latin ēvādō (“to pass or go over; flee”), from ē (“out of, from”) + vādō (“to go; walk”). See also wade.

s.def: To get away from by cunning; to avoid by using dexterity, subterfuge, address, or ingenuity; to cleverly escape from.

to evade the force of an argument

ety: Back-formation from evaluation.

s.def: To return or have a specific value.

ety: From French évaluation. By surface analysis, evaluate + -ion.

s.def: An assessment, such as an annual personnel performance review used as the basis for a salary increase or bonus, or a summary of a particular situation.

s.def: A completion of a mathematical operation; a valuation.

ety: From Middle English evaungel, evangile, from Old French evangile, from Late Latin evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news”), from εὐάγγελος (euángelos, “bringing good news”), from εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + ἀγγέλλειν (angéllein, “to announce”) (English angel). s.def: The Christian gospel.

An evangelist.

ety: From evangelic + -al, from Old French evangelique, from Latin evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news”).

ety: From Middle English [Term?], from Old French esvanir, compare Latin evanescere. See evanesce, vanish.

ety: First attested in 1545, borrowed from Latin ēvapōrātus, the perfect passive participle of ēvapōrō (“to evaporate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). ety: From Middle French évasion, from Late Latin evasionem (accusative of evasio).

s.def: The act of eluding or evading or avoiding, particularly the pressure of an argument, accusation, charge, or interrogation; artful means of eluding.

ety: From a variant of the Middle English noun even (itself from Old English ǣfen), with a pre-1200 loss of the terminal '-n', which was mistaken for an inflection. See also the now archaic or poetic even (“evening”), from the same source. In medieval Europe, days were considered to extend from sunset to sunset rather than midnight to midnight, so the night before a holiday was considered part of it, hence its "eve".

s.def: The day or night before, usually used for holidays, such as Christmas Eve.

s.def: Evening, night.

ety: From Middle French event, from Latin ēventus (“an event, occurrence”), from ēveniō (“to happen, to fall out, to come out”), from ē (“out of, from”), short form of ex + veniō (“come”); related to venture, advent, convent, invent, convene, evene, etc.
