ety: From Middle English examinen, examenen, from Old French examiner, from Latin exāmināre.

s.def: To observe carefully or critically to learn about someone or something.
ex: He examined the crime scene for clues.
She examined the hair sample under a microscope.
Well, nobody knows about the little things / Nobody knows what they really mean / Nobody ever wants to take the time / To examine what's on your mind

s.def: To check the health or condition of something or someone.
ex: The doctor examined the patient.

s.def: To determine the aptitude, skills or qualifications of someone by subjecting them to an examination.
To interrogate.
ex: The witness was examined under oath.

s.def: An act of examining.
ex: Soutar scratched the back of his neck then had a quick examine of his nails. Deep-ingrained purple they were.

ety: From Middle English example, exaumple, from Old French example, essaumple, from Latin exemplum (“sample, pattern, specimen, copy for imitation, etc.”, literally “what is taken out”); see exempt. Doublet of exemplum and sample. Displaced native Middle English forebisne, from Old English forebȳsn; and Middle English bisne, from Old English bȳsn (modern English bizen).

s.def: Something that is representative of all such things in a group.
Something that serves to illustrate or explain a rule.
Something that serves as a pattern of behaviour to be imitated (a good example) or not to be imitated (a bad example).
ex: Nelson Mandela was an example for many to follow.
Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge,[…]

s.def: A person punished as a warning to others.
ex: […]hang him, hee'le be made an example.

s.def: A parallel or closely similar case, especially when serving as a precedent or model.
An instance (as a problem to be solved) serving to illustrate the rule or precept or to act as an exercise in the application of the rule.
To be illustrated or exemplified (by).
Alternative form of exanthem.

ety: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin exarchus.

s.def: In the Byzantine Empire, a governor of a distant province.
In the Eastern Christian Churches, the deputy of a patriarch, or a bishop who holds authority over other bishops without being a patriarch.
In these same churches, a bishop appointed over a group of the faithful not yet large enough or organized enough to constitute an eparchy or diocese.

ety: First attested in 1534; borrowed from Latin exasperātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin exasperō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex (“out of; thoroughly”) + asperō (“to make rough”), from asper (“rough”). Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

s.def: To tax the patience of; irk, frustrate, vex, provoke, annoy; to make angry.
ex: [S]he exasperates her security men by acting as if she were protected by some invisible shield.
News that Adam Crozier, Royal Mail chief executive, is set to receive a bumper bonus will exasperate postal workers.

s.def: Exasperated.
Exasperated; embittered.
ex: Like swallows which the exasperate dying year Sets spinning […]

s.def: To overaspirate the letter h, or to aspirate it whenever it begins a word, once a common form of hypercorrection.
Heat of passion; violent anger.
The state of being excandescent, of glowing with heat.

ety: First attested in 1599, from Latin excavātus (“hollowed out”), perfect passive participle of excavō (“to hollow out”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex (“out”) + cavō (“to hollow out, pierce”), from cavus (“cave, hole”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Participial usage up until Early Modern English.

s.def: To make a hole in (something); to hollow.
To remove part of (something) by scooping or digging it out.
To uncover (something) by digging.
Made hollow.
excavated, hollowed out
Any member of a major grouping of unicellular eukaryotes, of the clade Excavata.

ety: From Latin excavātiō (“a hollowing out”), from excavō (“to hollow out”), from ex + cavō (“to hollow out”), from cavus (“hollow”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewh₁- (“vault, hole”). Equivalent to excavate + -ion.

s.def: The act of excavating, or of making hollow, by cutting, scooping, or digging out a part of a solid mass.
ex: Near-synonyms: hollowing out, hollowing

s.def: Something uncovered by archaeological excavation.
ex: To date, [Taco's 1982 cover of Irving Berlin's 1935] "Cheek To Cheek" and similar auditory excavations have fared poorly.

s.def: A cavity formed by cutting, digging, or scooping.
An uncovered cutting in the earth, in distinction from a covered cutting or tunnel.
The material dug out in making a channel or cavity.
ex: […] to cart away the excavations from the work, and to recart the same back again so far as required to fill the trench over the sewer […]

s.def: Archaeological research that unearths buildings, tombs and objects of historical value.
A site where an archaeological exploration is being carried out.
The act of discovering and exposing or developing (a quality).
ex: Chua looks at the landscape of childhood rather like a mining engineer looks at a pristine landscape—ripe for the excavation of talent.
This Andrade, a lawyer, seemed to enjoy bureucratic process as much as Mário de Andrade valorized the enthnographic excavation of creativity.

ety: From excavate + -or.

s.def: A vehicle, often on tracks, used to dig ditches etc.
A person who excavates.
ex: the excavators of an ancient Egyptian tomb

s.def: A curette used to scrape out pathological material.

ety: From Middle English exceden, from Old French exceder, from Latin excēdō (“to go beyond”), from ex- (“out, forth”) with cēdō (“to go”); see cede and compare accede etc. Partly displaced native Old English ofersteppan, whence Modern English overstep.

s.def: To be larger, greater than (something).
ex: The company's 2005 revenue exceeds that of 2004.

s.def: To be better than (something).
ex: The quality of her essay has exceeded my expectations.
Descriptions of nature that far exceed anything else we've heard.

s.def: To go beyond (some limit); to surpass; to be longer than.
ex: Your password cannot exceed eight characters.
Name the time, but let it not / Exceed three days.

s.def: To predominate.
To go too far; to be excessive.
ex: And to speak impartially, old Men, from whom we should expect the greatest example of Wisdom, do most exceed in this point of folly […].

ety: From Middle English excellen, from Old French exceller, from Latin excellere, excelsum; ex (“out”) + *cellō, an unattested verb root found in culmen (“height, top”); Compare French exceller. See also culminate, column.

s.def: To surpass someone or something; to be better or do better than someone or something.
ex: I excelled everyone else with my exam results.
Compositions which follow the style of Nissi Belzer's creations in structure but which excel them in length.

s.def: To do much better than usual.
ex: Everyone agreed Magnus really excelled himself this tournament.

s.def: To be much better than others.
ex: But it is as a destroyer of grasshoppers that the dickcissel excels.

s.def: To exceed, to go beyond.
ex: She opened; but to shut / Excelled her power: the gates wide open stood […]
I reason, we could die : / The best vitality / Cannot excel decay; / But what of that?

ety: From Middle English excellence, from Old French excellence, from Latin excellentia.

s.def: The quality of being excellent; brilliance
ex: John Davies was awarded for excellence in the field of computer security.

s.def: Something in which one excels.
An excellent or valuable quality; something at which any someone excels; a virtue.

ety: From Middle English excellencie, from Latin excellentia.

s.def: Synonym of excellence; the quality of being excellent.
A form of address for certain high officials or dignitaries.

ety: From Middle English excellent, from Old French excellent, from Latin excellēns (“elevated, exalted”), present participle of excellō (“elevate, exult”), equivalent to excel + -ent.

s.def: Of higher or the highest quality; splendid.
Having excelled, having surpassed.
Exceptionally good of its kind.
ex: Bill and Ted had an excellent adventure last week in preparation for their history exam.

s.def: Superior in kind or degree, irrespective of moral quality.
ex: Elizabeth, therefore, who was an excellent hypocrite
Their sorrows are most excellent.

s.def: Excellently.

der: my very excellent mother just served us…

ety: From Latin excelsior, comparative of excelsus (“high”). The name of the stuffing material was originally a trademark. As an exclamation, originating in Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's poem Excelsior (1841), based on the New York state motto. Popularized in the comic book fandom by Marvel Comics editor Stan Lee, who chose the term to sign off his columns as it was an obscure term and would confound competing publishers who imitated his style.

s.def: Loftier, yet higher, more elevated; ever upward.
ex: All we know for certain is that our tree, now approaching a hundred years old, was excelsior – loftier than any other ash in the vicinity.

s.def: More surpassing, more excelling.
ex: It was clear from the first three paragraphs that the language employed by Mr Tolkien was excelsior. He was brilliant.

s.def: Onward; a rallying cry for progress.
ex: ... and when the shout 'Excelsior!' echoed, up the oaken heights, Two hundred heels went thundering all at once, Four stairs at every jump
The bishops cried: "Excelsior!" But the archbishop: "Stay!"

s.def: A greeting, farewell or acclamation.
ex: MARTIN PRINCE: Finally, Bart's one of us! NERDS: Excelsior!

s.def: The size of type between Norse and brilliant, standardized as 3-point.
Stuffing material (as for furniture and mattresses) made of slender, curled woodshavings, as a substitute for hair.
ex: Each Pet Rock came in a cardboard carrying case, complete with air holes, tenderly nestled on a bed of excelsior.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French excepter, from Latin exceptus.

s.def: To exclude; to specify as being an exception.
ex: I find most people annoying — present company excepted, of course!
But this [ban on circumcision] must have been a provocation, as the emperor Antoninus Pius later acknowledged by excepting the Jews.

s.def: To take exception, to object (to or against).
ex: to except to a witness or his testimony
Yea, but methinks I hear some man except at these words […].

s.def: Used to introduce an exception or qualification to something previously stated.
ex: There was nothing in the cupboard except a tin of beans.
Except that he is wearing polka-dot drawers, he is buck naked.

s.def: Used to introduce a clause, phrase, verb infinitive, adverb or other non-noun complement forming an exception or qualification to something previously stated.
ex: You look a bit like my sister, except (that) she has longer hair.
I never made fun of her except teasingly.
To survive, I did everything except steal.

s.def: Loosely, used to introduce a contrastive statement explaining why something wasn't successful, didn't happen, etc.
ex: They fired tear gas at us, except the wind was blowing the wrong way.
I almost walked out, except I remembered the promise I had made.

s.def: Unless; used to introduce a hypothetical case in which an exception may exist.
ex: And they sayde: We have no moo but five loves and two fisshes, except we shulde goo and bye meate for all this people.
Offensive wars, except the cause be very just, I will not allow of.
I am […] not so clear how you will be able to avoid it, except you assert the independence to which your estate gives you a title.

Old French excepcion Anglo-Norman excepciounbor. Middle English exception Engl…

s.def: The act of excepting or excluding; exclusion; restriction by taking out something which would otherwise be included, as in a class, statement, rule.
ex: the exception of a rule

s.def: An interruption in normal processing, typically caused by an error condition, that can be raised (“thrown”) by one part of the program and handled (“caught”) by another part.
ex: null pointer exception

s.def: that which is excepted or taken out from others
That which is excluded from others; a person, thing, or case, specified as distinct, or not included.
ex: That rule is usually true, but there are a few exceptions.

s.def: An objection, on legal grounds; also, as in conveyancing, a clause by which the grantor excepts or reserves something before the right is transferred.
An objection; cavil; dissent; disapprobation; offense; cause of offense.
To throw an exception.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰ Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs Proto-Italic *eks Latin ex Latin ex- substratebor.? Old French excepcion Anglo-Norman excepciounbor. Middle English exception Engl…

s.def: Liable to cause disapproval, objection or debate.
ex: The subject however is rendered still more exceptionable by the aukward and ridiculous manner in which it is here treated.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰ Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs Proto-Italic *eks Latin ex Latin ex- substratebor.? Old French excepcion Anglo-Norman excepciounbor. Middle English exception Engl…

s.def: Forming an exception; not ordinary; uncommon; rare.
ex: What an exceptional meal!

s.def: Better than the average; superior due to exception or rarity.
ex: The quality of the beer was exceptional.

s.def: Corresponding to something of lower dimension under a birational correspondence.
ex: an exceptional curve; an exceptional divisor

s.def: An exception, or something having an exceptional value

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰ Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs Proto-Italic *eks Latin ex Latin ex- substratebor.? Old French excepcion Anglo-Norman excepciounbor. Middle English exception Engl…

s.def: The belief that something (a nation, species etc.) is exceptional, superior, or does not conform to an established norm.
The state of being special, exceptional or unique.
A philosophy of prevention or of intervention.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰ Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs Proto-Italic *eks Latin ex Latin ex- substratebor.? Old French excepcion Anglo-Norman excepciounbor. Middle English exception Engl…

s.def: without exception
Without the use of an exception-handling mechanism.

ety: From Latin excerptus, past participle of excerpere (“to pick out”), from ex (“out”) + carpere (“to pick, pluck”).

s.def: A clip, snippet, passage or extract from a larger work such as a news article, a film, or a literary composition.
To select or copy sample material (excerpts) from a work.
ex: out of which we have excerpted the following remarkable particulars

ety: From Middle English exces (“excess, ecstasy”), from Old French exces, from Latin excessus (“a going out, loss of self-possession”), from excedere, excessum (“to go out, go beyond”). See exceed.

s.def: The state of surpassing or going beyond a limit; the state of being beyond sufficiency, necessity, or duty; more than what is usual or proper.
ex: The excess of heavy water was given away to the neighbouring country.
I leaped up in an excess of enthusiasm.
To gild refined gold, to paint the lily, To throw a perfume on the violet, […] Is wasteful and ridiculous excess.

s.def: The degree or amount by which one thing or number exceeds another; remainder.
ex: The difference between two numbers is the excess of one over the other.

s.def: An act of eating or drinking more than enough.
ex: And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess.

s.def: Spherical excess, the amount by which the sum of the three angles of a spherical triangle exceeds two right angles. The spherical excess is proportional to the area of the triangle.
A condition on an insurance policy by which the insured pays for a part of the claim.
More than is normal, necessary or specified.
To declare (an employee) surplus to requirements, such that he or she might not be given work.

ety: From Middle English eschaunge, borrowed from Anglo-Norman eschaunge, from Old French eschange (whence modern French échange), from the verb eschanger, from Vulgar Latin *excambiāre (from Latin ex with Late Latin cambiō). Spelling later changed on the basis of ex-, with pronunciation following. By surface analysis, ex- + change.

s.def: An act of exchanging or trading.
ex: All in all, it was an even exchange.
an exchange of cattle for grain
I'll help you out this time, depending on what can you give me in exchange.

s.def: A place for conducting trading.
ex: The stock exchange is open for trading.
The old corn exchange has been converted into a music venue.

s.def: Ellipsis of telephone exchange.
ex: The 555 exchange is reserved for use by the phone company, which is why it's often used in films.
NPA-NXX-1234 is standard format, where NPA is the area code and NXX is the exchange.

s.def: A conversation.
ex: After a lengthy exchange with the manager, we were no wiser.

s.def: The loss of one piece and associated capture of another.
The thing given or received in return; especially, a publication exchanged for another.
ex: Lady, as you are mine, I am yours, I giue away my selfe for you, and doat vpon the exchange.

s.def: The transfer of substances or elements like gas, amino-acids, ions etc. sometimes through a surface like a membrane.
The difference between the values of money in different places.
Clipping of exchange of contracts.
To trade or barter.
ex: I'll gladly exchange my place for yours.

s.def: The rate at which one currency may be exchanged for another currency.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *tek- Proto-Indo-Iranian *kšáyati Proto-Iranian *xšáyati Old Persian 𐏋 (XŠ) Middle Persian 𐭬𐭫𐭪𐭠 (mlkʾ) Classical Persian شاه (šāh)bor. Arabic شَاه (šāh)bor. Latin scaccus Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -ārium Medieval Latin scaccarium Anglo-Norman eschekerbor. Middle English escheker English exchequer From Middle English escheker, from Anglo-Norman escheker (“chessboard”), from Medieval Latin scaccarium. This is…

s.def: An office of revenue taxation; a treasury.
An available fund of money, especially one for a specific purpose.
To proceed against (a person) in the Court of Exchequer.

ety: From Middle Dutch excijs, altered under the influence of Latin excisus (“cut out, removed”), from earlier accijs (“tax”), from Old French acceis (“tax, assessment”) (whence modern French accise), from Vulgar Latin *accensum, ultimately from Latin ad + census (“tax, census”).

s.def: A tax charged on goods produced within the country (as opposed to customs duties, charged on goods from outside the country).
To impose an excise tax on something.
To cut out; to remove.
ex: Military censors have excised some details from the photographs for security reasons.
[T]hey [warts] may be lifted up with the forceps, and excised with a knife or scissors, and the wound touched with nitrate of silver.

ety: Etymology tree English excite Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Old French -ablebor. Middle English -able English -able English excitable From excite + -able.

s.def: Easily excited.
ex: The excitable puppy jumped all over the furniture.

s.def: Able to respond to external stimuli.
Able to be promoted to an excited state.

ety: From Middle English excitacion, excitacioun, from Old French excitation, from Latin excitātiō. Morphologically excite + -ation.

s.def: The act of producing excitement (stimulation); also, the excitement produced.
ex: I'm pickin' up good vibrations / She's giving me the excitations.

s.def: A transition of a nucleus, atom or molecule to an excited state by the absorption of a quantum of energy; the opposite of relaxation.
The activity produced in an organ, tissue, or part, such as a nerve cell, as a result of stimulation.
The act of exciting or putting in motion; the act of rousing up or awakening.

ety: From Middle English exciten, from Old French exciter, from Latin excitō (“to call out, call forth, arouse, wake up, stimulate”), frequentative of excieō (“to call out, arouse, excite”), from ex (“out”) + cieō (“to call, summon”). See cite and compare to accite, concite, incite.

s.def: To stir the emotions of; to cause to feel excitement.
ex: The fireworks which opened the festivities excited anyone present.

s.def: To arouse or bring out (e.g. feelings); to stimulate.
ex: Favoritism tends to excite jealousy in the ones not being favored.
The political reforms excited unrest among the population.
Smugglers operating secretly so as not to excite suspicion.

s.def: To cause an electron to move to a higher than normal state; to promote an electron to an outer level.
ex: By applying electric potential to the neon atoms, the electrons become excited, then emit a photon when returning to normal.

s.def: To energize (an electromagnet); to produce a magnetic field in.
ex: to excite a dynamo

ety: From excite + -ed.

s.def: Having great enthusiasm, passion and energy.
ex: He was very excited about his promotion.
Yesterday was Thursday, Thursday / Today i-is Friday, Friday / We-we-we so excited / We so excited / We gonna have a ball today

s.def: Being in a state of higher energy.
ex: The excited electrons give off light when they drop to a lower energy state.

s.def: Having an erection; erect.
Sexually aroused.
ex: When you lick my neck like that, I get really excited, baby!

ety: From Middle English excitement, from Old French excitement, equivalent to excite + -ment.

s.def: The state of being excited (emotionally aroused).
ex: to get caught up in the excitement
By late accounts from Rotterdam, that city seems to be in a high state of philosophical excitement.
Elise nodded, fighting the traitorous flutters of excitement in her stomach.

s.def: Something that excites.

ety: Etymology tree English excite Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English exciter From excite + -er.

s.def: One who or that which excites.
The electronic oscillator that generates the carrier signal for a transmitter.

An audio signal processing technique used to enhance a signal by dynamic equalization, phase manipulation, harmonic synthesis of (usually) high frequency signals, and the addition of subtle harmonic distortion.
Creating or producing excitement.
ex: Some of the most exciting games ever played have ended in draws.

s.def: Sexually stimulating.
Alternative form of exciter.

ety: From Middle French exclamer, from Latin exclāmō, exclāmāre (“call out”), from ex- + clāmō (“to call”).

s.def: To cry out suddenly, from some strong emotion.
ex: I am a soldier, and unapt to weep, Or to exclaim on fortune’s fickleness.
Very grave and good Women exclaimed against Men who begot Children and then disowned them.
This wretched note was the finale of Emma’s breakfast. When once it had been read, there was no doing any thing, but lament and exclaim.

s.def: To say suddenly and with strong emotion.
ex: You never pump your arm when you score, you never exclaim anything, you don’t even smile when you fire a perfect backhand straight down the line.

s.def: Exclamation; outcry, clamor.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French exclamation, from Latin exclāmātiō, from exclāmō (“to cry out”) + -tiō.

s.def: A loud calling or crying out, for example as in surprise, pain, grief, joy, anger, etc.
A word expressing outcry; an interjection.
An exclamation mark.
The punctuation mark “!” (generally used to denote excitement, surprise or shock).
ex: The excessive use of exclamation marks devalues their effect, but is typical of concise genres such as cartoons, not reference works!
Traditionally, the exclamation mark has been used sparingly, especially in formal writing.

ety: Borrowed from Latin exclūdō, from prefix ex- (“out”) + variant form of verb claudō (“close”).

s.def: To bar (someone or something) from entering; to keep out.
To expel; to put out.
ex: to exclude young animals from the womb or from eggs

s.def: To omit from consideration.
ex: Count from 1 to 30, but exclude the prime numbers.

s.def: To refuse to accept (evidence) as valid.
To eliminate from diagnostic consideration.

ety: From Middle English exclusion, exclusioun, from Old French [Term?] and Latin exclusiō, from exclūdō. By surface analysis, exclude + -sion.

s.def: The act of excluding or shutting out; removal from consideration or taking part.
The act of pushing or forcing something out.
An item not covered by an insurance policy.

ety: From Latin exclūsīvus, from excludere (“to shut out, exclude”), from ex- (“out”) + variant form of verb claudere (“to close, shut”).

s.def: Excluding items or members that do not meet certain conditions.
Referring to a membership organisation, service or product: of high quality and/or renown, for superior members only.
A snobbish usage, suggesting that members who do not meet requirements, which may be financial, of social status, religion, skin colour etc., are excluded.
ex: Exclusive clubs tend to serve exclusive brands of food and drinks, in the same exorbitant price range, such as the 'finest' French châteaux.

s.def: Exclusionary.
Whole, undivided, entire.
ex: The teacher's pet commands the teacher's exclusive attention.

s.def: Of or relating to the first-person plural pronoun when excluding the person being addressed.
ex: The pronoun in "We're going to a party later, but you aren't invited" is an exclusive "we".

s.def: Having a romantic or sexual relationship with one another, to the exclusion of others.
ex: They decided to no longer be exclusive.

s.def: Information (or an artefact) that is granted or obtained exclusively.
ex: The editor agreed to keep a lid on a potentially disastrous political scoop in exchange for an exclusive of a happier nature.

s.def: A member of a group who excludes others from their society.
ex: The exclusives at the English Universities apply the term CAD to all non-members.

s.def: A word or phrase that restricts something, such as only, solely, or simply.

ety: From Latin excōgitāre, from ex- + cōgitāre (“think”).

s.def: To think over something carefully; to consider fully; cogitate.
ex: Did he ponder the harmony of the spheres? Certainly not: celestial spheres were first excogitated decades or more after Pythagoras' death.

s.def: To reach as a conclusion through reason or careful thought.
ex: After many years of study, he excogitated a solution.
This evidence […] thus excogitated out of the general theory.

ety: From Ecclesiastical Latin excommunicātus, perfect passive participle of excommunicō (“excommunicate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, ex- + communicate.

s.def: To officially exclude someone from membership of a church or religious community.
To exclude from any other group; to banish.
ex: Although our Macs served us well, in those early, dark years Macintosh users were effectively excommunicated by the computer establishment.

s.def: Excommunicated.
An excommunicated person.

ety: From Middle English excommunicacion, from Late Latin excommūnicātiō. By surface analysis, excommunicate + -ion. Displaced native Old English āmǣnsumung.

ety: From Middle English expedient, from Old French expedient, from Latin expediens (stem expedient-), present participle of expedire (“to bring forward, to dispatch, to expedite; impers. to be profitable, serviceable, advantageous, expedient”), from ex (“out”) + pēs (“foot, hoof”).

s.def: Expeditious, quick, rapid.
Suitable to effect some desired end or the purpose intended.
ex: Most people, faced with a decision, will choose the most expedient option.
Nothing but the right can ever be the expedient, since that can never be true expediency which would sacrifice a greater good to a less.

s.def: Affording short-term benefit, often at the expense of the long-term.
Governed by self-interest, often short-term self-interest.
A method or means for achieving a particular result, especially when direct or efficient; a resource.
ex: To secure such a market, there is no other expedient, than to promote manufacturing establishments.
He would never let her know that he was aware of the strange expedient to which she had been driven by her great distress.
Depressingly, [...] the expedient of importing African slaves was in part meant to protect the native American population from exploitation.

ety: From Latin expedītus (“unimpeded, unfettered”), perfect passive participle of expediō (“bring forward, set right”).

s.def: To accelerate the progress of.
ex: He expedited the search by alphabetizing the papers.

s.def: To perform (a task) fast and efficiently.
To perform the duties of an expediter.
To free from impediment; to release or set at liberty.
Free of impediment; unimpeded.
ex: […] to make the way plaine and expedite […]

s.def: Expeditious; quick; prompt.
ex: nimble and expedite […] in its operation

ety: From expedite + -er.

s.def: A person who expedites.
Employee charged with tasks related to the purchase of materials (place orders, receive shipments, examine deliveries, check correctness of invoices) and other clerical duties.

ety: From Middle French expédition, and its source, Latin expeditio.

s.def: An important or long journey, for example a march or a voyage.
A military journey; an enterprise against some enemy or into enemy territory.
A trip, especially a long one, made by a person or a group of people for a specific purpose.
ex: a naval expedition
a scientific expedition
an expedition across the Alps

s.def: The group of people making such excursion.
The process or activities of performing expediter tasks.
The quality of being expedite; speed, quickness.
ex: one of them began to come nearer our boat than at first I expected; but I lay ready for him, for I had loaded my gun with all possible expedition […].
he presently exerted his utmost agility, and with surprizing expedition ascended the hill.
He saw the same Turnkey unfetter a man / With but little expedition, / Which put him in mind of the long debate / On the Slave-trade abolition.

s.def: The act of expediting something; prompt execution.
To take part in a trip or expedition; to travel.

ety: From Middle English expedycius (“useful, fitting”), from Latin expedītus (“disengaged, ready, convenient, prompt; unfettered, unencumbered”), past participle of expediō.

s.def: Fast, prompt, speedy.
ex: Near-synonym: expedited
Our coachman and horses are so extremely expeditious!—I believe we drive faster than anybody.

s.def: Completed or done with efficiency and speed; facilitating speed.
ex: Near-synonym: expedited
Now, there was a sort of rough-and-ready law in Ireland in those days which was of great convenience to persons desirous of expeditious justice[…].

ety: Late Middle English: from Latin expellere, from ex- (“out”) + pellere (“to drive”).

s.def: To eject.
To remove from membership.
ex: He was expelled from school multiple times for disruptive behaviour.

s.def: To deport.
To fire (a bullet, arrow etc.).
ex: But to the ground the idle quarrell fell: / Then he another and another did expell.

ety: Borrowed from Latin expendō (“to weigh; to pay out”). Doublet of spend.

s.def: To consume, exhaust (some resource).
ex: If my death might make this island happy […] I would expend it with all willingness.
Here Black expends an important tempo. 11...B-K3 seems better.
To handle the unceasing traffic increase, immense sums of money are being expended in dealing with bottlenecks.

ety: From stem of Medieval Latin expenditus, irregular perfect passive participle of expendō (“to weigh, to pay out”), + -ure (“process or result”).

s.def: Act of expending or paying out.
The amount expended; expense; outlay.
ex: The expenditure of time, money, and political capital on this project has been excessive.

ety: From Middle English expense, from Anglo-Norman expense and Old French espense, from Late Latin expēnsa, from Latin expendō. See expend. Doublet of speso.

s.def: A spending or consuming, often a disbursement of funds.
ex: She went to great expense to ensure her children would get the best education.
Buying the car was a big expense, but will be worth it in the long run.
We had a training weekend in New York, at the expense of our company.

s.def: The elimination or consumption of something, sometimes with the notion of loss or damage to the thing eliminated.
ex: Jones reached the final at the expense of Smith, who couldn't beat him.

s.def: Loss.
ex: And moan the expense of many a vanished sight.

s.def: To charge a cost against an expense account; to bill something to the company for which one works.
ex: It should be acceptable to expense a business lunch with a client.

ety: From Latin *expēnsīvus, from expendō (“to weigh out (money), to pay out”) (whence English expend). By surface analysis, expense + -ive. In the sense of "high-priced" has largely displaced dear.

s.def: Having a high price or cost.
ex: In Starbucks’s case, the firm has in effect turned the process of making an expensive cup of coffee into intellectual property.

s.def: Taking a lot of system time or resources.
ex: an unnecessarily expensive choice of algorithm

s.def: Given to expending a lot of money; profligate, lavish.
ex: 'His character is now before you — expensive, dissipated, and worse than both […]'

s.def: Having a high economy rate.

ety: Etymology tree English expensive Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English expensiveness From expensive + -ness.

s.def: The state of being expensive; the entailing of great expense.

ety: From Middle English experience, from Old French, from Latin experientia (“a trial, proof, experiment, experimental knowledge, experience”), from experiens, present participle of experiri (“to try, put to the test, undertake, undergo”), from ex (“out”) + peritus (“experienced, expert”), past participle of *periri (“to go through”); see expert and peril. Displaced native Old English āfandung (“experience”) and āfandian (“to experience”).

s.def: The effect upon the judgment or feelings produced by any event, whether witnessed or participated in; personal and direct impressions as contrasted with description or fancies; personal acquaintance; actual enjoyment or suffering.
ex: It was an experience he would not soon forget.

s.def: A collection of events and/or activities from which an individual or group may gather knowledge, opinions, and skills.
ex: they knew soone by experience how slenderly guarded against danger, the majestie of Rulers is

s.def: The knowledge thus gathered.
An activity one has performed.
A business offering in which a major focus is the way that the customer interacts with the business throughout the transaction, as opposed to only its outcome (the product or service).
Synonym of experience points
ex: As your troops conquer the enemy, they'll earn experience and gain levels. Each time they level up, their stats will increase.

s.def: Trial; a test or experiment.
ex: She caused him to make experience / Vpon wyld beasts, which she in woods did find, / With wrongfull powre oppressing others of their kind

s.def: To observe certain events; undergo a certain feeling or process; or perform certain actions that may alter one or contribute to one's knowledge, opinions, or skills.

ety: From experience + points.

s.def: A system of points which, when a predetermined amount is accumulated by a player character, causes them to level up. This is one of the core mechanics of many role-playing games.
ex: He got a few experience points by killing two zombies and two spiders.

ety: From Latin experientiālis, from experientia + -ālis.

s.def: Of, related to, encountered in, or derived from experience.
ex: Near-synonym: empirical
Atheists argue that there is no experiential confirmation for the existence of a god.
Each color has a unique experiential quality.

ety: From Middle English experiment, from Old French esperiment (French expérience), from Latin experimentum (“experience, attempt, experiment”), from experior (“to experience, to attempt”), itself from ex + *perior, in turn from Proto-Indo-European *per-.

s.def: A test under controlled conditions made to either demonstrate a known truth, examine the validity of a hypothesis, or determine the efficacy or likelihood of something previously untried.
ex: conduct an experiment
carry out some experiments
perform a scientific experiment

s.def: Experience, practical familiarity with something.
ex: Pilot [...] Vpon his card and compas firmes his eye, The maisters of his long experiment, And to them does the steddy helme apply [...].

s.def: To conduct an experiment.
ex: We're going to experiment on rats.

s.def: To experience; to feel; to perceive; to detect.
ex: The Earth, the which may have carried us about perpetually ... without our being ever able to experiment its rest.

s.def: To test or ascertain by experiment; to try out; to make an experiment on.
ex: Til they had experimented whiche was trewe, and who knewe most.

s.def: To try something to observe the results.
ex: I want to experiment with psychedelics.

ety: Inherited from Middle English expert, derived from Old French expert (“experienced”), espert, from Latin expertus (contracted from *experitus), perfect active participle of experior (“to try”), from ex- + *-perior.

s.def: Extraordinary capable or knowledgeable.
ex: I am expert at making a simple situation complex.
My cousin is an expert pianist.

s.def: Characteristic of an expert.
ex: This problem requires expert knowledge.

s.def: Proven, experienced, veteran.
A person with extensive knowledge or ability in a given subject.
ex: If an expert says it can't be done, get another expert. - David Ben-Gurion
We called in several experts on the subject, but they couldn't reach an agreement.
I'm an expert in my field Ufology, yes, it's all real Ancient aliens, it's all true I'm an expert just like you

s.def: A player ranking just below master.
To have (something) reviewed or checked by an expert.
ex: Estimated cost of editorial work on Advanced History […] Estimated cost of experting the Advanced History […]

s.def: A witness that has expertise in a certain field.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰ Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs Proto-Italic *eks Latin ex Latin ex- Proto-Indo-European *perh₃-der. Proto-Italic *parjō Latin pariō Latin experior Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Italic *-tos Latin -tus Latin expertusder. French expert French -ise French expertisebor. English expertise Borrowed from French expertise. Compare gourmandise.

s.def: Great skill or knowledge in a particular field or hobby.
ex: He spoke of Scotland's hydroelectric projects in Africa, local expertise shared with the world's poor.

s.def: Advice, or opinion, of an expert.
To supply with expert knowledge or advice.
ex: Since 1979, we have developed a method for expertising the design of the processes and improving them.
Including a plurality of different expertise in the decision-making processes corresponds to expertising the democratic procedures.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰ Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs Proto-Italic *eks Latin ex Latin ex- Proto-Indo-European *pewH- Proto-Italic *pīos Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Proto-Italic *-ājō Proto-Italic *-āō Proto-Italic *pīāō Latin piō Latin expiō ▲ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂tos Proto-Italic *-ātos…

s.def: To atone or make reparation for.
ex: The Treasurer obliged himself to expiate the injury.
Thus those pious souls who expiate the remainder of their sins amidst such tortures will receive a special and opportune consolation, […]
I am going out to expiate a great wrong, Paul. A very necessary feature of the expiation is the marksmanship of my opponent.

s.def: To make amends or pay the penalty for.
ex: He had only to live and expiate in solitude the crimes which he had committed.

s.def: To relieve or cleanse of guilt.
ex: […] and Epimenides was brought from Crete to expiate the city.

s.def: To purify with sacred rites.
To wind up, bring to an end.

ety: From Middle French expiation, from Latin expiātiō(n) (“satisfaction”).

s.def: An act of atonement for a sin or wrongdoing.
ex: And see far off below you, where the gulf is fixed, / Your persecutors, in timeless torment, / Parched passion, beyond expiation.

s.def: The act of expiating or stripping off.
ex: expiation of his immanities fore.

ety: From Middle English expiracioun, exspiracioun (“vapor, breath”), from Latin expīrātiōnem, exspīrātiōnem, accusative singular of expīrātiō, exspīrātiō. By surface analysis, expire + -ation.

s.def: An act, process, or instance of expiring.
ex: Holonym: respiration
crackles heard on expiration

ety: From Middle English expire, from Middle French expirer, from Latin expīrō, exspīrō, from ex- (“out”) + spīrō (“breathe, be alive”).

s.def: To die.
ex: The patient expired in hospital.
People bled to death like gentlemen in an operating room or expired without comment in an oxygen tent.

s.def: To lapse and become invalid.
ex: My library card will expire next week.

s.def: To come to an end; to conclude.
ex: And when the thousand yeeres are expired, Satan shall be loosed out of his prison, […]

s.def: To exhale; to breathe out.
ex: Anatomy exhibits the lungs in a continual motion of inspiring and expiring air.
This chafed the boar; his nostrils flames expire.
Animals expire carbon and plants inspire it; plants expire oxygen and animals inspire it.

s.def: To give forth insensibly or gently, as a fluid or vapour; to emit in minute particles.
ex: the expiring of cold out of the inward parts of the earth in winter

s.def: To bring to a close; to terminate.
ex: Expire the term / Of a despised life.

s.def: To cause to lapse; to invalidate.
ex: The site expires cached pages that are older than 24 hours.

ety: From expire + -y.

s.def: End; termination; expiration.
ex: approaching expiry
The contract becomes void upon expiry.

s.def: Synonym of expiration date.
Death.
The date on which something runs out or expires and becomes out of date, in many cases requiring renewal.
ex: The expiry date of my debit card is the 30th of April.
You'd better throw that milk out: it's passed the expiry date.

ety: From Middle English explanen, from Old French explaner, from Latin explanō (“to flatten, spread out, make plain or clear, explain”), from ex- (“out”) + planō (“to flatten, make level”), from planus (“level, plain”); see plain and plane. Compare esplanade, splanade. Displaced Old English reċċan.

s.def: to make intelligible
To make plain, manifest, or intelligible; to clear of obscurity; to illustrate the meaning of.
ex: The issue was explained to the governor in detail.

s.def: To give the reason for, justification for, or cause of.
To make flat, smooth out.
To unfold or make visible.
To make something plain or intelligible.
ex: She tried to explain but he wouldn’t listen.
Like their Western counterparts, local media engages in shorthand - it reports rather than explains.

ety: From Latin explanatio (“an explanation, interpretation”), from explanare (“explain”); see explain. Morphologically explain + -ation. Displaced native Old English racu.

s.def: The act or process of explaining.
ex: The explanation was long and drawn-out.

s.def: Something that explains or makes understandable.
ex: An explanation for the UFO sightings was easily found.

s.def: A resolution of disputed points pursuant to discussion; a mutual clarification of disputed points; reconciliation.
ex: This little explanation with Mr. Knightley gave Emma considerable pleasure.

ety: From Late Latin explānātōrius, from Latin explānāt-, past-participle stem of explānāre (“to explain”). Displaced Old English ġereclīċ.

s.def: Intended to serve as an explanation.
ex: Below the diagram is an explanatory text.

s.def: Disposed to explain.

ety: From Late Latin explētīvus (“serving to fill out”), from Latin explētus, the perfect passive participle of expleō (“fill out”), itself from ex (“out, completely”) + *pleō (“fill”).

s.def: Serving to fill up, merely for effect, otherwise redundant.
Marked by expletives (phrase-fillers).
A profane, vulgar term, notably a curse or obscene oath.
ex: If we don't take advantage of any [expletive] in any way, then it's our loss.

s.def: A word without meaning added to fill a syntactic position.
A word that adds to the strength of a phrase without affecting its meaning (such as fucking in "there's no fucking way he's gonna get away with it").
An obscene or otherwise offensive interjection (such as shit, fuck, or damn it).

ety: Borrowed from Latin explicāre (“unfold, explain”).

s.def: To explain meticulously or in great detail.
ex: My homework is to explicate a poem.
Isou himself, enemy of all conventional discourse, wrote hundreds, then thousands of pages explicating his theories; […]

s.def: Evolved; unfolded.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French explication and its etymon Latin explicātiō, explicātiōnem. By surface analysis, explicate + -ion.

s.def: The act of opening or unfolding.
The act of explaining; an explanation.
ex: Her anthemic "Who Stands For Life" is a powerful explication of what it means to be "pro-life".

s.def: The sense given by an expositor.

ety: Borrowed from French explicite, from Latin explicitus (“disentangled, easy”), variant of explicātus.

s.def: Very specific, clear, or detailed.
ex: I gave explicit instructions for him to stay here, but he followed me, anyway.

s.def: Containing material (e.g. language or film footage) that might be deemed offensive or graphic through clear and direct expressions.
ex: The film had several scenes including explicit language and sex.

s.def: The final few words of a text.
Used at the conclusion of a book to indicate the end.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰ Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs Proto-Italic *eks Latin ex Latin ex- Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂-? Proto-Indo-European *pel-? Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂-u-h₂- Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂-u-d- Latin plaudō Latin explōdōbor. English explode First recorded around 1538, from the Latin verb explōdere (“drive out or off by clapping”). The meaning was originally theatrical, "to drive an actor off the stage by maki…

s.def: To fly apart with sudden violent force; to blow up, to burst, to detonate, to go off.
ex: The bomb explodes.

s.def: To destroy with an explosion.
ex: The assassin exploded the car by means of a car bomb.

s.def: To make a violent or emotional outburst; to suddenly give expression to powerful and often negative or unpleasant emotion, especially anger.
ex: She exploded when I criticised her hat.
“Nonsense!” Jack exploded at me. “Why Miss Bertram here knocked that theory into a cocked hat coming over on the train.”

s.def: To increase suddenly.
ex: When pigeons can come to a spot day in and day out for a guaranteed meal, their populations explode.
Despite these products typically costing more, the market for organic food has exploded over the last couple of decades.

s.def: To increase arbitrarily or boundlessly.
ex: The function f(x) = 1/x explodes around x = 0.

s.def: To destroy violently or abruptly.
ex: They sought to explode the myth.

s.def: To create an exploded view of.
ex: Explode the assembly drawing so that all the fasteners are visible.

s.def: To disprove or debunk.
ex: Astrology is required by many famous physicians […] doubted of, and exploded by others.

s.def: To emerge suddenly.
ex: to explode into the mainstream; to explode onto the scene

s.def: To ejaculate.

ety: From Old French esploit (noun), esploitier (verb).

s.def: A heroic or extraordinary deed.
An achievement.
ex: The first trek to the summit of Mount Everest was a stunning exploit.

s.def: A program or technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability in other software.
ex: For example, you can create PE files that are valid PDF exploits or valid ZIP files, valid JPG files, and so on.

s.def: An action or technique that takes advantage of the conditions of a video game to gain an advantage, or to disadvantage others.
To use (something) to someone's advantage, such as one's own benefit or a society's benefit.
ex: to exploit natural resources in a sustainable way

s.def: To make unfair use of someone else's labor, person, or property to one's own advantage.
ex: Materialistic people who exploit others will come to a bad end.

ety: From Old French exploitable or exploit + -able.

s.def: Easily fooled; credulous.
Able to be exploited, especially commercially.

ety: Borrowed from French exploitation, from exploiter (“exploit”), from Latin explicō (“unfold, deploy”). By surface analysis, exploit + -ation.

s.def: The act of utilizing something; industry.
ex: the exploitation of natural resources

s.def: The improper use of something for selfish purposes.
ex: the exploitation of children in beauty pageants

s.def: The act or result of forcibly depriving someone of something to which they have a right.
ex: Undocumented migrants are vulnerable to exploitation.

s.def: The marketing and promotion of a film.
ex: This territory continued to be the greatest field for the exploitation and distribution of our films non-theatrically, […]
The difference is that obtaining increased financial input during the production phase of the film reduces the risk during the exploitation phase.

s.def: A genre of media focused on lurid depictions of topical social issues such as violence, sexuality and marginalized groups.
ex: It is here that we arrive at the main question of this paper: can an exploitation director be an auteur?

ety: From Middle French exploration, from Latin exploratio. Morphologically explore + -ation.

s.def: The process of exploring.
ex: By this time, largely inspired by The Railway Magazine, I had begun to spread my wings, and had started on a long career of railway exploration.

s.def: The process of penetrating, or ranging over for purposes of (especially geographical) discovery.
ex: The exploration of unknown areas was often the precursor to colonization.

s.def: The (pre-)mining process of finding and determining commercially viable ore deposits (after prospecting), also called mineral exploration.
A physical examination of a patient.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰ Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs Proto-Italic *eks Latin ex Latin ex- Latin plōrō Latin explōrōder. Middle French explorerder. English explore From Middle French explorer, from Latin explōrāre (“to investigate, search out”), itself said to be originally a hunters' term meaning "to set up a loud cry", from ex- (“out”) + plōrāre (“to cry”), but the second element is also explained as "to make to flow" (from pluere (“to flow”)). Displace…

s.def: To examine or investigate something systematically.
ex: The committee has been exploring alternative solutions to the problem at hand.

s.def: To travel somewhere in search of discovery.
ex: It was around that time that the expedition began exploring the Arctic Circle.

s.def: To examine diagnostically.
To (seek) experience first hand.
ex: It is normal for a boy of this age to be exploring his sexuality.

s.def: To seek for something or after someone.
To be engaged exploring in any of the above senses.
ex: He was too busy exploring to notice his son needed his guidance.

s.def: To wander without any particular aim or purpose.
ex: The boys explored all around till cold and hunger drove them back to the campfire one by one.

s.def: To seek sexual variety, to sow one's wild oats.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰ Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs Proto-Italic *eks Latin ex Latin ex- Latin plōrō Latin explōrōder. Middle French explorerder. English explore Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English explorer From explore + -er.

s.def: A person who by means of travel (notably an expedition) searches out new information.
One who explores something
Any of various hand tools, with sharp points, used in dentistry.
A visual representation of a file system etc. through which the user can navigate.

ety: From French explosion, from Latin explōsiōnis, genitive form of explōsio, from explōdo (“to drive out by clapping”), from ex- and plōdo (“to clap or strike”). For more information see explode.

s.def: A violent release of energy (sometimes mechanical, nuclear, or chemical); an act or instance of exploding.
ex: A man was injured by an explosion caused by drilling into a missed shot at the Mendota mine above Silver Plume, Colo.

s.def: The sound of an explosion.
A sudden, uncontrolled or rapid increase, expansion, or bursting out.

ety: From Latin explōs-, stem of the perfect passive participle of explōdō + the suffix -ive.

s.def: Able to, or likely to, explode.
ex: an explosive device

s.def: Having the character of an explosion.
ex: an explosive fire

s.def: Easily driven to anger, usually with reference to a person.
ex: He has an explosive personality.

s.def: Rapidly accelerating.
ex: Near-synonym: plyometric
explosive movements

s.def: Shocking; startling.
ex: an explosive accusation

s.def: Synonym of plosive.
ex: the explosive consonants

s.def: Any explosive substance.
A plosive.

ety: From Latin expōnēns, present participle of expōnō (“to expose; to exhibit, display, set out; to explain”), from ex- (“out, away”) + pōnō (“to lay, place, put”).

s.def: One who expounds, represents or advocates.
ex: Like attracts like," explained Mrs. Mailey, who was quite as capable an exponent as her husband.

s.def: The number by which a value (called the base) is said to be raised to a power in exponentiation: for example, the 3 in 2³=8.
The degree to which the root of a radicand is found, for example, the 2 in ^(2])√=b.
A phonological manifestation of a morphosyntactic property; in layman's terms, the expression of one or more grammatical properties by sound.
The part of a floating-point number that represents its exponent value.

ety: Etymology tree English exponent Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisder. Old French -ialder. Middle English -ial English -ial English exponential From exponent + -ial.

s.def: Expressed in terms of an exponent (power of a base), the base often being 10 or e.
ex: In base-10 exponential form, 1,000,000 is written as 10⁶.
If not otherwise specified, "the" exponential function is normally understood to mean eˣ.

s.def: having a high or rapid rate of change

Characterised by a rate of change that is proportional to the value of the varying quantity, or, equivalently, by a doubling or halving over successive fixed intervals of time or other parameter, described as exponential growth or exponential decay.
ex: There were two deaths on Monday, four on Tuesday, and eight on Wednesday. The rate of increase seems exponential.

s.def: Characterised by a very rapid rate of change, especially increase, or merely a very large amount or degree.
ex: Near-synonyms: extreme, huge
There's been an exponential rise in the number of crimes reported this year, compared to last year.

s.def: The growth in the value of a quantity in which the rate of growth is proportional to the instantaneous value of the quantity; for example, when the value has doubled, the rate of increase will also have doubled. The rate may be positive or negative.
Very rapid growth.

ety: From Latin exportare.

s.def: Of or relating to exportation or exports.
The act of exporting.
ex: The export of fish is forbidden in this country.

s.def: Something that is exported.
ex: Oil is the main export of Saudi Arabia.

s.def: To carry away.
ex: [They] export honour from a man, and make him a return in envy.

s.def: To sell (goods) to a foreign country.
ex: Japan exports electronic goods throughout the world.
Jim is a nurseryman, specialising in clematis, and he has built up a business exporting 150 varieties to countries all over the world.

s.def: To cause to spread in another part of the world.
To send (data) from one program to another.
To put up (a child) for international adoption.

ex: India is the leading exporter of guar gum, making up nearly 85 per cent of the global production.

ety: From Middle English exposen, from Old French exposer (“to lay open, set forth”), from Latin expōnō (“set forth”), with contamination from poser (“to lay, place”). Doublet of expone and expound (via Old French espondre (“to set forth, explain”)), from the same Latin term.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French exposé.

The act of exposing somebody or something; a shameful showing up.
A formal recital or exposition.
Open (especially to something), unconcealed and/or unprotected (and therefore vulnerable, susceptible).

an exposed path (trail, etc) up the mountain (one with a drop-off on one or both sides)

ex: The film was not exposed to sufficient light.

ety: From Middle English exposicioun, from Old French esposicion, from Latin expositiō, from expōnere (“to put forth”). The sense meaning "exhibition" is a later semantic loan from French exposition.

The act of expulsion, or being expelled, from a place.
An exhibition, especially of goods, artwork or cultural displays to the public.

The abandonment of an unwanted child.
A person who expounds; a commentator.

ety: From Latin expostulō (“demand, claim”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, ex- + postulate.

s.def: The act of exposing something, such as a scandal.
The degree to which an individual, their content, or their brand is seen by the target market or the general public; internet fame.
The act or condition of being at risk of financial losses.
That part which is facing or exposed to something, e.g. the sun, weather, sky, or a view.
ex: They rented a cabin with a beautiful southern exposure.

s.def: An instance of taking a photograph.
The piece of film exposed to light.
Details of the time and f-number used.
The amount of sun, wind etc. experienced by a particular site.

ety: From Middle English expounden, from Old French espondre, from Latin exponere. Doublet of expone and expose.

s.def: To set out the meaning of; to explain or discuss at length.

s.def: To make a statement, especially at length.
ex: He expounded often on the dangers of the imperial presidency.

ety: From French exprès, from Latin expressus, past participle of exprimere (see Etymology 2, below).

s.def: A mode of transportation, often a train, that travels quickly or directly, either on a regular schedule or as a special or excursion. Express trains often pass through stations along the way without stopping at them.
ex: I took the express into town.

s.def: A service that allows mail or money to be sent rapidly from one destination to another.
An express rifle.
ex: "Give me my express," I said, laying down the Winchester, and he handed it to me cocked.

s.def: A clear image or representation; an expression; a plain declaration.
A messenger sent on a special errand; a courier.
An express office.
ex: She charged him […] to ask at the express if anything came up from town.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French expression, from Late Latin expressiō, expressiōnem (“a pressing out”). Morphologically express + -ion.

A colloquialism or idiom.

ex: They stared at the newcomer with a puzzled expression.

s.def: An arrangement of symbols denoting values, operations performed on them, and grouping symbols.
A piece of code in a high-level language that returns a value.
The action of expressing thoughts, ideas, feelings, etc.

A specific blend of whisky.
The act of pressing or squeezing out.

Able to represent a number of ideas or concepts.
ex: A programming language that is Turing complete is more expressive than one that is not.

s.def: Any word or phrase that expresses (that the speaker, writer, or signer has) a certain attitude toward or information about the referent.

A word or phrase, belonging to a distinct word class or having distinct morphosyntactic properties, with semantic symbolism (for example, an onomatopoeia), variously considered either a synonym, a hypernym or a hyponym of ideophone.
ex: I examine the valency of expressives, a class of ideophones in Mundari, comparing their behaviors as predicates to those of reduplicated verb forms.

s.def: Exclusively or specifically.

ety: From express + -man.

ety: From express + way.

Synonym of freeway.

ety: From Middle English expulsioun, from Old French expulsion, from Latin expulsio, expulsionem.

ex: The publisher decided to expurgate the love scene from the book, to make it more child-friendly.

ex: The publisher decided to expurgate the book, which meant removing the love scene.

ety: From Latin exquīsītus (“to be outsought”), perfect passive participle of exquīrō (“to outseek”).

The inability to perceive multiple stimuli simultaneously.
